title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
造未具安得髦士而烝之臣
用是懼滋甚雖然上之化下
若均埏埴士之從上猶金在
鎔顧士生當時所尚殊術三
代貴德其士賢西漢崇儒明
理亂其士知後漢師章句其
士守名檢隋唐重吏道其士
===
通宋顓經義其士近正
國朝兼所尚方聞之士莫不斌
斌烈於往古第風會以漸而
趨本眞既久則斲飾羽成畫
破觚爲圓始未嘗不樸茂後
習稍靡也
主上紹隆丕緒瑩精太平

國朝兼所尚方聞之士莫不斌
斌烈於往古第風會以漸而
趨本眞旣久則斲飾羽成畫
破觚爲圓始未嘗不樸茂後
習稍靡也
主上紹隆丕緒瑩精太平
punctuated: 造未具，安得髦士而烝之？臣用是懼滋甚。雖然，上之化下，若均埏埴；士之從上，猶金在鎔。顧士生當時，所尚殊術：三代貴德，其士賢；西漢崇儒明理亂，其士知；後漢師章句，其士守名檢；隋唐重吏道，其士通；宋顓經義，其士近正。國朝兼所尚，方聞之士，莫不斌斌烈於往古。第風會以漸而趨，本眞既久，則斲飾羽成畫，破觚爲圓，始未嘗不樸茂，後習稍靡也。主上紹隆丕緒，瑩精太平，
translation_en: …when the cultivation is not yet complete, how could we obtain eminent scholars and advance them? Because of this, your servant's apprehension grows all the greater. Even so, the ruler's transformation of those below is like the potter's wheel shaping clay, and scholars' following of the ruler is like metal in the mold. Yet for scholars born in a given age, what is esteemed follows different paths: the Three Dynasties prized virtue, so their scholars were worthy; the Western Han revered Confucian learning and clarified order and disorder, so its scholars were wise; the Later Han took chapter-and-verse commentary as its master, so its scholars upheld moral reputation and conduct; the Sui and Tang valued the way of administrative service, so their scholars were versatile; the Song focused exclusively on the meaning of the Classics, so its scholars approached rectitude. Our Dynasty combines what was esteemed by all of them, and scholars of broad learning are without exception refined and accomplished, outshining antiquity. However, customs and trends shift gradually over time: when pristine genuineness has endured for long, it becomes carved away, adorning feathers to make a picture and paring down corners to make circles; what in the beginning was never other than simple and flourishing later becomes somewhat decadent in practice. His Majesty has succeeded to and exalted the great patrimony, polishing his spirit for Supreme Peace…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
思以大治濯俗則設象為紀所
厲中外臣工甚具不數歲間
聲敎布濩盈溢天區士皆懍懍
爭祓濯其心宅於醇粹語有
之千里而一士比肩也累時
而有賢士接軫也故士者衆
人之尤賢士者衆尤之尤其
===
尤彌出其道彌博一邑之雋
於郡為輩一郡之第於天下
為根今士獲於表簿而材於
巖廊出郡邑而天下矣其曷
以為天下用其道在返質在
務實曩歲主司執是以諗多
士士瞿然顧化亦皆質有其
alt_text:
思以大治濯俗則設象爲紀所
屬中外臣工甚具不數歲聞
聲教布濩盈溢天區士皆廩廩
爭祓濯其心宅於醇粹語有
之千里而一士比肩也累時
而有賢士接軫也故士者衆
人之尤賢士者衆尤之尤其
===
尤彌出其道彌慱一邑之雋
於郡爲輩一郡之第於天下
爲棖令士獲於表薄而材於
巖廓出郡邑而天下矣其曷
以爲天下用其道在返質在
務實曩歲主司執是以諗多
士士瞿然顧化亦皆質有其
punctuated: 思以大治濯俗，則設象為紀，所厲中外臣工甚具。不數歲間，聲敎布濩，盈溢天區，士皆懍懍，爭祓濯其心，宅於醇粹。語有之：「千里而一士，比肩也；累時而有賢士，接軫也。」故士者，衆人之尤；賢士者，衆尤之尤。其尤彌出，其道彌博。一邑之雋，於郡為輩；一郡之第，於天下為根。今士獲於表簿，而材於巖廊，出郡邑而天下矣，其曷以為天下用？其道在返質，在務實。曩歲主司執是以諗多士，士瞿然顧化，亦皆質有其
translation_en: … intending to cleanse popular customs through grand governance, He has established standards as guidelines, and the measures by which He encourages officials both inside and outside the capital are thoroughly complete. Within just a few years, His moral prestige and transformative teaching have spread far and wide, filling the realm under heaven. Scholars all stand in reverent awe, vying to purify and cleanse their minds and abide in unadorned purity. As the saying goes: "If there is one scholar in a thousand li, it is as if they stand shoulder to shoulder; if worthy scholars appear across successive ages, it is as if their carriage-crossbars touch one another." Therefore, a scholar is the finest among the multitude, and a worthy scholar is the finest among the finest. The more outstanding his excellence, the broader his Way. The outstanding talents of a single district become peers within a prefecture; the successful candidates of a single prefecture form the root for the entire empire. Now that these scholars have been recorded on the registers of merit and are to serve as capable timber in the lofty halls of court, they have emerged from their prefectures and districts onto the stage of the empire—how then shall they make themselves of use to the empire? The Way lies in returning to substance and in devoting oneself to practical reality. In recent years, the examiners held fast to this principle to admonish the multitude of scholars; the scholars, startled into reflection, turned toward transformation, and all likewise came to possess substance along with their…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
文夫業旣返質而就實則効
用有基矣臣不敢緩頰稱前
說敢以効用之術進古之事
君者必先服能然後任故學
古入官未聞以仕學也今所
學誦者前人緒餘所簡進者
叔時文藝師迹不達變趨儷
===
不存志緣故不博聞法律與
詩書其途兩譚說與厝注其
體二故有臨民而墻面剸務
而岐心有久而稍更有僨於
始而卒不振非才頓知不及
也爲不狎習也蓋足未嘗行
堯禹問曲折目未嘗見墨翟
alt_text:
文夫業既返質而就實則効
用有基矣臣不敢縷縷稱前
說敢以効用之術進古之事
君者必先服能然後任故學
古入官未聞以仕學也今所
學誦者前人緒餘所簡進者
叔時文藝師迹不達變趨儺
===
不存志緣故不博聞法律與
詩書其途兩譚說與層注其
體二故有臨民而墻面剸務
而岐心有久而稍更有債於
始而卒不振非才頓知不及
也爲不狎習也蓋足未嘗行
堯禹間曲折目未嘗見墨翟
punctuated: 文。夫業旣返質而就實，則効用有基矣。臣不敢緩頰稱前說，敢以効用之術進。古之事君者，必先服能然後任，故學古入官，未聞以仕學也。今所學誦者，前人緒餘；所簡進者，叔時文藝。師迹不達變，趨儷不存志，緣故不博聞。法律與《詩》《書》，其途兩；譚說與厝注，其體二。故有臨民而墻面，剸務而岐心；有久而稍更，有僨於始而卒不振。非才頓知不及也，爲不狎習也。蓋足未嘗行，堯、禹問曲折；目未嘗見，墨翟
translation_en:
… refinement. Now that their studies have already returned to unadorned simplicity and turned toward practical substance, there is a foundation for rendering effective service. Your servant dares not wag his tongue repeating earlier arguments, but ventures instead to present the art of rendering effective service.

In antiquity, those who served their ruler necessarily first cultivated competence in their duties and only afterward assumed office; thus one "studied antiquity in order to enter office," and it was never heard that one learned how to govern by holding office. Nowadays, what scholars study and recite are the leftover dregs of predecessors; what they are selected and promoted for are the literary crafts of a decadent age. Imitating outward traces, they do not comprehend how to adapt to change; pursuing parallel prose, they do not preserve high aspirations; clinging to routine precedents, they do not broaden their learning. Laws and statutes on the one hand, and the Odes (Shi) and Documents (Shu) on the other, go along two separate paths; theoretical discussion and practical administration have two distinct forms. Consequently, there are those who, upon taking charge of the people, stand as if facing a blank wall, and who, when cutting through official business, are of divided mind; there are those who only after a long time become slightly experienced, and those who ruin things at the outset and in the end never recover. This is not because their talent is dull or their intelligence falls short; it is because they are not practiced and familiar with the work. Indeed, where the feet have never walked, even Yao and Yu would have to ask about the twists and turns; what the eyes have never seen, even Mo Di …

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
所重于士者上之以道德次
以功能卓然崛起于世世自
奇之耳士不以炫騖而求庸
也士惟無奇而欲以奇見則
必崇竑其論議而競非常可
喜之績蕩侈踰檢託之乎恢
弘虛憍恃氣託之乎豪特凌
===
厲詷察託之乎高明騷屑紛
更託之乎敢任乃有背棄師
說軼而之典常之外者而眾
相慕好因謂之奇則躍冶為
祥金而覂駕為良驥無乃非
國家求士意乎是故察名實者
戒矯飾求聰明者先平淡質

punctuated: 所重于士者，上之以道德，次以功能，卓然崛起于世，世自奇之耳，士不以炫騖而求庸也。士惟無奇而欲以奇見，則必崇竑其論議，而競非常可喜之績。蕩侈踰檢，託之乎恢弘；虛憍恃氣，託之乎豪特；凌厲詷察，託之乎高明；騷屑紛更，託之乎敢任。乃有背棄師說，軼而之典常之外者，而眾相慕好，因謂之奇，則躍冶為祥金，而覂駕為良驥，無乃非國家求士意乎？是故察名實者戒矯飾，求聰明者先平淡。質
translation_en: …what is valued in a scholar-official is, above all, moral virtue, and secondarily, practical accomplishment. When he rises preeminently in the world, the world will naturally regard him as extraordinary; a scholar does not seek employment through flashy display and restless ambition. Only when a scholar lacks anything truly extraordinary and yet wishes to distinguish himself by being extraordinary will he inevitably make his arguments grandiose and compete for unusual, crowd-pleasing achievements. Unrestrained extravagance that transgresses bounds is passed off as broad-minded magnanimity; hollow arrogance that relies on bluster is passed off as heroic uniqueness; harshness and prying scrutiny are passed off as lofty brilliance; and restless meddling that disrupts established ways is passed off as bold responsibility. There are even those who abandon the teachings of their masters and stray beyond normal standards and constant principles, yet the crowd admires and delights in one another for doing so, thereby calling it extraordinary. By that logic, metal that leaps wildly from the smelting pot would be considered auspicious bronze, and a horse that throws off its harness and overturns the carriage would be considered a fine steed—surely this is not the Dynasty's intention in seeking out scholars! Therefore, those who examine name and reality guard against pretentious artifice, and those who seek true discernment put plainness first. Substantial…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
行闇修屋漏無忝不必奇節
孳孳公上之急臨事而辦不
必奇勳盡心守法無失忠順
臣之所望于士者止此耳且
夫身事
明主奮庸
清夷之世至幸也經訓在前
===
律令在後
成憲在
朝清議在野至嚴也雖有抱關
之能挈缾之智慮無不自效
而况士哉士愼勗之使人謂
士習之淳自茲舉始則臣有
榮藉無尚以臣之說爲卑卑
alt_text:

===

成憲在
朝清議在野至嚴也雖有抱關
之能挈缾之智慮無不自效
而況士哉士愼勗之使人謂
士習之淳自茲舉始則臣有
榮藉無尙以臣之說爲卑卑
punctuated: 行闇修，屋漏無忝，不必奇節；孳孳公上之急，臨事而辦，不必奇勳；盡心守法，無失忠順，臣之所望于士者，止此耳。且夫身事明主，奮庸清夷之世，至幸也；經訓在前，律令在後，成憲在朝，清議在野，至嚴也。雖有抱關之能、挈缾之智，慮無不自效，而况士哉！士愼勗之，使人謂士習之淳自茲舉始，則臣有榮藉，無尚以臣之說爲卑卑
translation_en: …practice and cultivate oneself in obscurity, incurring no shame even in the most secluded corners of one's house—one does not need extraordinary moral heroism; to attend tirelessly to the urgent needs of the state and the sovereign, managing affairs effectively as they arise—one does not need extraordinary martial or administrative exploits; to devote one's whole heart to abiding by the law, never failing in loyalty and obedience—what your servant hopes for from the scholars is nothing more than this. Moreover, to personally serve an enlightened sovereign and rise through meritorious service in an age of peace and tranquility is the greatest of good fortune; with the teachings of the Classics before one and the statutes and ordinances behind, the established institutions at court and pure public opinion in the countryside, the standards are most strict. Even those with merely the ability of a gatekeeper or the wisdom of one who carries a water jar presumably never fail to exert themselves in service—how much more so the scholars! Let the scholars carefully exert themselves in this, so that people will say that the return to purity in literati customs began with this examination. Then your servant will have reason to feel honored and supported; do not still regard your servant's words as commonplace and…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
無竒也是役也同考試則洗
馬臣子義侍讀臣萬化修撰
臣繼臯編修臣鵬程臣訥臣
懋德臣虞夔臣鈳臣孟麟檢
討臣應元臣楚先都給事中
臣燿臣光啓給事中臣彥郎
中臣浴德臣檄主事臣樓監
===
試則御史臣鯨臣功而防檢
于外則御史臣王國臣甘雨
例得並書
資政大夫禮部尚書兼文淵
閣大學士申時行謹序

無竒也。是役也，同考試則洗馬臣子義、侍讀臣萬化、修撰臣繼臯、編修臣鵬程、臣訥、臣懋德、臣虞夔、臣鈳、臣孟麟、檢討臣應元、臣楚先、都給事中臣燿、臣光啓、給事中臣彥、郎中臣浴德、臣檄、主事臣樓；監試則御史臣鯨、臣功；而防檢于外則御史臣王國、臣甘雨，例得並書。
資政大夫、禮部尚書兼文淵閣大學士申時行謹序。

…and unremarkable. In this assignment, the Associate Examiners were Librarian (Xianma) Your servant Ziyi 子義; Academician Reader-in-Waiting (Shidu) Your servant Wanhua 萬化; Senior Compiler (Xiuzhuan) Your servant Jigao 繼臯; Junior Compilers (Bianxiu) Your servant Pengcheng 鵬程, Your servant Ne 訥, Your servant Maode 懋德, Your servant Yukui 虞夔, Your servant Ke 鈳, and Your servant Menglin 孟麟; Examining Editors (Jiantao) Your servant Yingyuan 應元 and Your servant Chuxian 楚先; Chief Supervising Secretaries (Du Jishizhong) Your servant Yao 燿 and Your servant Guangqi 光啓; Supervising Secretary (Jishizhong) Your servant Yan 彥; Bureau Directors (Langzhong) Your servant Yude 浴德 and Your servant Xi 檄; and Bureau Secretary (Zhushi) Your servant Lou 樓. Monitoring the examination were Censors (Yushi) Your servant Jing 鯨 and Your servant Gong 功; and guarding and inspecting on the outside were Censors Your servant Wang Guo 王國 and Your servant Gan Yu 甘雨; by precedent they are all recorded together here.

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
子貢問曰何如斯可謂之士矣子曰行己
有恥使於四方不辱君命可謂士矣曰
敢問其次曰宗族稱孝焉鄉黨稱弟焉
曰敢問其次曰言必信行必果硜硜然
小人哉抑亦可以爲次矣
子曰回之爲人也擇乎中庸得一善則拳
拳服膺而弗失之矣
===
我亦欲正人心息邪說距詖行放淫辭以
承三聖者豈好辯哉予不得已也
易
象曰天行健君子以自彊不息
上九鼎玉鉉大吉无不利象曰玉鉉在上
剛柔節也
夫易廣矣大矣以言乎遠則不禦以言乎
邇則靜而正以言乎天地之間則備矣
夫乾其靜也專其動也直是以大生焉

夫乾其靜也專其動也直是以大生□
punctuated:
第壹場
四書
子貢問曰：「何如斯可謂之士矣？」子曰：「行己有恥，使於四方，不辱君命，可謂士矣。」曰：「敢問其次？」曰：「宗族稱孝焉，鄉黨稱弟焉。」曰：「敢問其次？」曰：「言必信，行必果，硜硜然小人哉！抑亦可以爲次矣。」
子曰：「回之爲人也，擇乎中庸，得一善，則拳拳服膺而弗失之矣。」
「我亦欲正人心，息邪說，距詖行，放淫辭，以承三聖者；豈好辯哉？予不得已也。」
易
《象》曰：「天行健，君子以自彊不息。」
上九，鼎玉鉉，大吉，无不利。《象》曰：「玉鉉在上，剛柔節也。」
夫《易》廣矣，大矣！以言乎遠則不禦，以言乎邇則靜而正，以言乎天地之間則備矣。夫乾，其靜也專，其動也直，是以大生焉。
translation_en:
First Session

The Four Books

Zigong asked, "What must a man be like so that he may be called an officer (shi)?" The Master said, "He who in his conduct of himself maintains a sense of shame, and when sent to any of the four quarters does not disgrace his ruler's commission, deserves to be called an officer." Zigong said, "May I venture to ask about the next grade?" The Master said, "He whom his clan praises for filial piety, and whom his fellow villagers praise for brotherly respect." Zigong said, "May I venture to ask about the next grade?" The Master said, "He whose words are insistently trustworthy and whose actions are insistently resolute—what an obstinate little man he is! Yet perhaps he too may be considered the next grade."

The Master said, "This was the manner of Hui as a man: he chose the Mean (Zhongyong), and whenever he attained a single good thing, he clasped it firmly to his breast and never lost it."

"I too wish to rectify men's hearts, put an end to perverse doctrines, oppose one-sided actions, and banish licentious expressions, so as to carry on the work of the three sages. How could I be fond of disputing? I have no alternative."

Book of Changes (Yi)

The Commentary on the Images (Xiang) says: "The movement of heaven is full of power; thus the superior man makes himself strong and untiring."

Nine at the top: The cauldron (Ding) has rings of jade. Great good fortune. Nothing that is not advantageous. The Commentary on the Images says: "Rings of jade at the top: the firm and the yielding meet in due proportion."

Now the Changes is broad indeed, and great indeed! If we speak of it in terms of what is far, it knows no bounds; if we speak of it in terms of what is near, it is still and right; if we speak of it in terms of the space between heaven and earth, it is all-complete. Now as for Qian, in its stillness it is concentrated, and in its movement it is straight; therefore it produces the great…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
夫坤其靜也翕其動也闢是以廣生焉
廣大配天地變通配四時陰陽之義配
日月易簡之善配至德
物相雜故曰文
書
予乘四載隨山刊木暨益奏庶鮮食予決
九川距四海濬畎澮距川暨稷播奏庶
艱食鮮食懋遷有無化居烝民乃粒萬
邦作乂
===
慎乃儉德惟懷永圖
無偏無陂遵王之義無有作好遵王之道
無有作惡遵王之路無偏無黨王道蕩
蕩無黨無偏王道平平無反無側王道
正直會其有極歸其有極
政貴有恒辭尚體要
詩
羔羊之皮素絲五紽退食自公委蛇委蛇
嗟爾君子無恒安處靖共爾位正直是與

punctuated:
夫坤，其靜也翕，其動也闢，是以廣生焉。廣大配天地，變通配四時，陰陽之義配日月，易簡之善配至德。
物相雜，故曰文。

書
予乘四載，隨山刊木，暨益奏庶鮮食。予決九川，距四海，濬畎澮，距川，暨稷播，奏庶艱食、鮮食。懋遷有無，化居。烝民乃粒，萬邦作乂。
慎乃儉德，惟懷永圖。
無偏無陂，遵王之義；無有作好，遵王之道；無有作惡，遵王之路。無偏無黨，王道蕩蕩；無黨無偏，王道平平；無反無側，王道正直。會其有極，歸其有極。
政貴有恒，辭尚體要。

詩
羔羊之皮，素絲五紽。退食自公，委蛇委蛇。
嗟爾君子，無恒安處。靖共爾位，正直是與。
translation_en:
…As for Kun (the Receptive), in its stillness it closes, and in its movement it opens; therefore, what is vast is produced from it. In vastness and greatness it matches Heaven and Earth; in variation and continuity it matches the four seasons; in the meaning of yin and yang it matches the sun and moon; and in the goodness of ease and simplicity it matches supreme virtue.
Things are intermingled with one another, and therefore they are called patterns.

Classic of Documents (Shu):
"I rode in my four conveyances, following the mountains and felling the trees, and together with Yi procured fresh meats for the multitudes. I opened the nine rivers to reach the four seas, and deepened the field ditches and canals to reach the rivers; and together with Ji sowed the grains, procuring for the multitudes hard-won food and fresh meats. I urged them to exchange what they had for what they had not, and to dispose of their accumulated stores. Then the multitude of people had grain to eat, and the myriad states were brought to order."
"Be cautious in your thrifty virtue, and cherish far-reaching plans."
"Without deflection, without unevenness, follow the royal righteousness; without indulging in personal likings, follow the royal way; without indulging in personal dislikings, follow the royal road. Without deflection, without partisanship, the royal way is broad and vast; without partisanship, without deflection, the royal way is level and smooth; without perversity, without one-sidedness, the royal way is straight and upright. Gather around the Supreme Standard; return to the Supreme Standard."
"In governance, constancy is prized; in proclamations, substance and conciseness are esteemed."

Classic of Odes (Shi):
"The skins of the lambs and sheep, with five braidings of white silk! They retire for their meal from the court, self-possessed and easy, self-possessed and easy."
"Oh, you noble men, do not constantly abide in ease! Quietly and reverently attend to your offices, and associate with the upright and straight. …"

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
神之聽之式穀以女
其胤維何天被爾祿君子萬年景命有僕
其僕維何釐爾女士釐爾女士從以孫
子
天命降監下民有嚴不僭不濫不敢怠遑
命于下國封建厥福
春秋
春齊侯宋人陳人蔡人邾人會于北杏莊
公十有三年秋七月辛巳豹及諸侯之
===
大夫盟于宋襄公二十有七年
夏六月宋公曹人邾人盟于曹南僖公十
有九年

What will be the continuation? Heaven invests you with dignity. For a myriad years, O sovereign, the great mandate stays attached to you. What is attached to it? You are granted heroic women; you are granted heroic women, and there follow descendants and sons.

“To cultivate one’s person and fulfill one’s words is called good conduct. When conduct is cultivated and words accord with the Way, that is the substance of ritual.”
“The Five Emperors took the aged as models: they nourished their vital breath and bodies without requesting words of counsel from them; yet when they had good acts or words, these were recorded to form trustworthy histories.”

“The Master said: ‘What the superior man calls benevolence—how difficult it is! The Book of Odes says: “The joyous and fraternal superior man is the father and mother of the people.” Joyously, he vigorously instructs them; fraternally, he delights them and gives them peace. Joyful without wildness, courteous yet affectionate, majestic and grave yet tranquil, filial and compassionate yet reverent—he causes the people to hold him in the esteem of a father and feel toward him the affection of a mother. Only when it is like this can one be the father and mother of the people. Without supreme virtue, who could be like this?’”

…gladly accepted them, earning praise for a thousand years—can they too be compared to antiquity? The foundational and flourishing enterprise of our dynasty far surpasses that of previous eras. Since His Majesty succeeded to the throne, laws have been cultivated and governance upheld, the seasons have been harmonious and goods abundant, the three frontiers are peaceful, and envoys speaking through multiple translators arrive in succession. In such an auspicious era and prosperous juncture, even what is praised in the Book of Odes (Shi) and the Book of Documents (Shu) could not surpass this! Yet those who dwell in Peace (Tai) dread the city wall collapsing back into the moat, and those who reside in Abundance (Feng) guard against the sun passing its zenith. Could it be that today there are no incipient sprouts or subtle stirrings of trouble that ought to be foreseen early and planned for in advance, so as to answer the teachings of the Book of Changes (Yi) and the Book of Documents (Shu)? His Majesty presently admires Yu and Zhou above, sharpening his spirit in pursuit of good governance. Should there be deep concerns and far-reaching counsels to mend and bolster this flourishing rule, even if they are vehement or excessive, He will gladly hear them in His tireless devotion from dawn to dusk. May you gentlemen set them forth candidly according to your thoughts, holding nothing back.

Only after it was established among the Erudites (boshi) in the Han dynasty did it begin to stand alongside the traditions of Gaotang Sheng 高堂生 and Xiao Fen 蕭奮 as one of the three ritual texts; down to Master Wang Zhongyan 王仲淹 [Wang Tong 王通] and Master Zhu Zhonghui 朱仲晦 [Zhu Xi 朱熹], they praised it repeatedly. However, the "Offices of Winter" (Dongguan) alone was missing, and Han scholars supplemented it with the Record of Trades (Kaogong ji); that this is uncanonical goes without saying. 問：儒者之說，尊周、孔而闢黃、老、申、韓，尚矣。乃史氏述二家，或以爲合于大道，或以爲南面之術，或取其明分職，或稱其輔禮制，于儒者則各有刺譏，何悖謬也？豈亦有見歟？即以漢事論：文帝躬脩玄默，其說出于黃、老，然致治之美，庶幾成、康；武帝尊儒術，黜百家，而其治顧不逮孝文遠甚，何歟？宣帝綜核名實，大抵申、韓術也，然號稱中興，與周宣侔德；元帝徵
translation_en:
…is intact and scattered among the other five offices, and others who say that the five offices appear interchangeably so the Office of Winter was never actually missing—how are we to adjudicate between them? Commentators consider it the book by which the former sages brought about Great Peace, which is right. Yet some composed a Summary of the Record (Lulüe) and some wrote Explanatory Meanings (Xunyi), while going awry in practical application; some applied five or six parts out of ten, and some applied eight or nine parts out of ten, yet the results in governance were remiss—why is this so? Master Cheng (Cheng Hao 程顥 / Cheng Yi 程頤) said: "Only when one has the spirit of the 'Ospreys' (Guanju) and the 'Toes of the Unicorn' (Linzhi) can one put into practice the institutions and laws of the Offices of Zhou (Zhouguan)." Then should those who exhaustively study the Classics today not also seek it by following that underlying spirit? I wish to examine and verify this together with you gentlemen, in order to observe your learning in investigating antiquity.

Question: In the doctrines of Confucians, honoring the Duke of Zhou and Confucius while refuting Huang-Lao (the Yellow Emperor and Laozi) and Shen-Han (Shen Buhai 申不害 and Han Fei 韓非) is of long standing. Yet when the historians recount these two schools, some consider them to accord with the Great Way, or to be the art of facing south as a ruler; some adopt their clarity in dividing official duties, or praise them for assisting the ritual system; whereas toward the Confucians they each have criticisms and ridicule. How perverse and mistaken this is! Or could it be that they too had some insight? Let us discuss this simply in terms of Han affairs: Emperor Wen personally cultivated mysterious quiescence, a doctrine derived from Huang-Lao, yet the beauty of the governance he achieved nearly equaled that of Kings Cheng and Kang of Zhou; Emperor Wu revered Confucian arts and dismissed the Hundred Schools, yet his governance on the contrary fell far short of the Filial Emperor Wen—why? Emperor Xuan comprehensively verified names and realities, which was by and large the art of Shen Buhai and Han Fei, yet his reign was acclaimed as a dynastic restoration, equal in virtue to King Xuan of Zhou; Emperor Yuan summoned…

問：文章與時高下，自古記之矣。歷觀盛世，其文皆溫厚雅馴，嗇于巧而安于朴。迨中葉，則學務多方，始競瑰奇、誇煒麗矣。顧浮文勝斯雅道傷，士習漸于澆薄。將文以時敝耶？抑文敝而世道從之耶？唐、宋之代，蓋有挽回而丕變之者，或以一人起八代之衰，或以一時正太學之體，功效何卓犖也！豈文固稟于風氣，而轉移化導，又人力使之然歟？明興二百餘年，文几幾變矣。蓋迄于今而稱盛際，其沿襲變易之槩，可略舉而言歟？今操觚之士，各欲縱其材情之所極，非
translation_en:
…summoned and employed Confucian scholars, entrusting them with state affairs, yet the achievements of Emperor Xiaoxuan declined under him. Where did the fault lie? Could it be that the Way of the Confucians was not even equal to that of Huang-Lao or Shen Buhai and Han Fei? Or is it that as the trends of the times progressed day by day, governance came to rely on laws and regulations, such that Huang-Lao and Shen-Han were all suited for practical use, whereas the Confucians actually had no bearing on order and disorder? Or is it rather a matter of whether they were employed well or poorly? Scholars value illuminating the Way and its methods and understanding the principles of governance; set forth the effects of these successes and failures in your essay.

Question: That literary composition rises and falls with the times has been recorded since antiquity. Looking through flourishing eras, their writing was consistently gentle, substantial, refined, and well-ordered, sparing in artifice and content in simplicity. By the middle periods, however, learning pursued multiple directions, and writers began to compete in the extraordinary and boast of brilliant ornateness. Yet when superficial rhetoric prevails, the refined Way is harmed, and the habits of scholars gradually sink into frivolity and shallowness. Does literature deteriorate because of the times, or does literature deteriorate first and the moral state of the world follow it? In the Tang and Song dynasties, there were indeed those who reversed this trend and brought about a great transformation: one man raised literature from the decline of eight dynasties, and another in a single moment rectified the literary style of the National University—how outstanding were their achievements! Could it be that while literature is indeed endowed by the prevailing ethos of the age, turning it around and guiding its transformation is nevertheless brought about by human effort? Since the rise of the Ming more than two hundred years ago, literary style has undergone several changes. Coming down to the present, which is hailed as a flourishing age, can you briefly recount the general outline of its continuities and transformations? Today, scholars who wield the writing tablet each wish to give full rein to the utmost limits of their talent and emotion; it is not…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
不爛焉可觀而論者復有文勝之慮抑
別有見歟玆欲華不滅質巧不斲朴以
無失先民之程則何術而可夫正文體
變士習
明詔所申飭諸士孰聞之矣願相與揚搉之
問中國之於夷狄順則撫之逆則威之此
制禦常道也史册所載未暇枚舉吾獨
惟夫漢建武永平之間勢足以鞭笞四
夷乃匈奴數寇邊求合市狡焉叵測猶
===
冀其通好而許之何怯也虜貢裘馬請
竽瑟不之予予弓矢刀劔何拙也虜旣
和矣而寇鈔不息和若不足恃矣然而
鄭衆不遣耿秉出屯虜再折北而北庭
遂空焉豈其和也固無妨于戰而和與
戰之權又在我而不在彼歟我
國家威德陋視漢代頃歲虜酋款塞乞貢市
願爲外臣廷議爭言非便迺
廟謨弘遠推赤心待之息兵罷警亦旣五六

不爛焉可觀，而論者復有文勝之慮，抑別有見歟？玆欲華不滅質，巧不斲朴，以無失先民之程，則何術而可？夫正文體、變士習，明詔所申飭，諸士孰聞之矣，願相與揚搉之。
問：中國之於夷狄，順則撫之，逆則威之，此制禦常道也。史册所載，未暇枚舉，吾獨惟夫漢建武、永平之間，勢足以鞭笞四夷，乃匈奴數寇邊，求合市，狡焉叵測，猶冀其通好而許之，何怯也？虜貢裘馬，請竽瑟，不之予，予弓矢刀劔，何拙也？虜旣和矣，而寇鈔不息，和若不足恃矣。然而鄭衆不遣，耿秉出屯，虜再折北，而北庭遂空焉。豈其和也固無妨于戰，而和與戰之權又在我而不在彼歟？我國家威德，陋視漢代。頃歲虜酋款塞，乞貢市，願爲外臣，廷議爭言非便。迺廟謨弘遠，推赤心待之，息兵罷警，亦旣五六
translation_en:
…not brilliantly impressive to behold, yet critics once again harbor concerns that ornate style is overpowering substance—or do they have some other insight? Now, if we wish for ornament not to extinguish substance, and artfulness not tohew away simplicity, so as not to lose the standards of the ancients, by what method may this be achieved? Rectifying literary style and transforming the habits of scholars is what the imperial edict has repeatedly admonished; you gentlemen are thoroughly familiar with this, and I wish to discuss and weigh it together with you.

Question: In China's dealings with the barbarians, pacifying them when they submit and overawing them when they rebel is the constant principle of control. What is recorded in the historical annals we have no leisure to enumerate one by one, but I reflect in particular upon the Jianwu [25–56 CE] and Yongping [58–75 CE] eras of the Han dynasty: their power was sufficient to whip the four barbarian peoples into submission, yet when the Xiongnu repeatedly raided the frontier and requested joint border markets, cunning and unfathomable as they were, the court still hoped for friendly relations and granted their request—how timid that was! When the caitiffs presented tribute of furs and horses and asked for reed pipes and zithers, the court did not give them those, but gave them bows, arrows, single-edged blades, and double-edged swords—how foolish that was! Once peace was made with the caitiffs, their raiding and plundering still did not cease, so it seemed that peace could not be relied upon. And yet when Zheng Zhong was no longer dispatched as envoy and Geng Bing went out to establish military colonies, the caitiffs were twice routed and driven north, and the Northern Court was consequently emptied. Could it be that making peace inherently posed no obstacle to waging war, and that the initiative for peace or war rested with us and not with them?

The prestige and virtue of our State look down upon the Han dynasty as paltry. In recent years, the caitiff chieftain knocked at the frontier passes, begging for tribute and markets and wishing to become an outer vassal. Discussions at court contended that this was inexpedient. Yet the imperial counsels of the ancestral temple were vast and far-reaching: treating them with utmost sincerity, we rested our troops and ended frontier alarms, and now five or six…

translation_en: … years now. Yet taking precautions before it rains is the supreme counsel of the state. Can the current arrangements for pacification and management through tribute and border markets, and the preparations for warfare and defense at the frontier commands, truly be relied upon? If the cunning caitiffs should break the covenant, would we be able to inflict a great blow upon them so that they dare not cast covetous eyes upon us? Among you many scholars there must be those who harbor foresight and concern ahead of time; assess the caitiffs' situation and devise plans for securing the future, for the authorities eagerly wish to hear them.

… in emergencies there is nothing that can be relied upon. Thus in antiquity there was no separate designation of "soldier" and yet military force was never neglected, whereas in later ages military forces were not abolished and yet the reality of military readiness was lost—a long-standing abuse! When our Dynasty established [its institutions?], there was nothing in the system that was not admirable, yet today one or two aspects have somewhat slackened. Allow me to speak of this in detail.

At the founding of the Dynasty, when the imperial rule was established and grandly occupied a position of strategic command, the weighty armies of the realm were gathered and stationed in garrison at the Capital in order to strengthen the trunk and weaken the branches, while the various prefectures and the frontiers each had their own commands. Those commanding in the Capital never crossed over to oversee the frontier prefectures, which would have stripped away their own imperial guard formations (gouchen); those stationed in the frontier prefectures rotated on duty to go up to guard, linked together in unbroken ranks to solidify the defense of [the Capital?]. Moreover, [there was no?] transferring of prefectural troops to garrison the frontiers or having frontiers mutually garrison one another; in this way […], the military camps and ramparts were kept ever clear in their roles and free of disorder. In recent years, however, [the military practices?] generally fall into four categories: rotating conscripts (gengzu), frontier garrison conscripts (yaoshu), [supplemental?] corvée troops, and recruits (zhaomu)—which are also remnants of middle antiquity. Under the Han, the Northern and Southern Armies were transferred from the commanderies and kingdoms, rotating once a year and holding a general review in autumn; today's shift-training troops (bancao jun) from the Central Capital (Zhongdu), Henan, and Shandong are just like this. Yet they frequently suffer from hard physical labor. At first they were temporarily borrowed for construction service by the state, and later this gradually spread even to great families, where they are promiscuously used as laborers, and the exactions for hiring substitutes and commutation fees are excessively burdensome. How can they bear this? Those originally called upon to report for training in two seasonal shifts were meant to shoulder halberds and cross blades—yet instead they are put to work with baskets and spades! Under the Han, soldiers who went in person to garrison the frontiers each had their statutes on rotation; the troops from Yansui and Ningxia today who enter to guard the Capital (ruwei jun) are just like this [read: 今 for 令]. This was not in the original statutory code. In past times, when …

translation_en:
…when the interior suffered caitiff raids, because the troops of Jizhou were untrained, these frontier forces were temporarily borrowed to create a pincer formation of mutual support. Yet they go on service without respite, and when their term is up no one replaces them; trudging through mud on circuitous routes, they are exhausted from rushing to obey orders. This was a temporary expedient—why has it gone so long without being reversed? In Liaodong there is the practice of levying supplementary conscripts, which also reflects the Han-dynasty principle of sending even the old, weak, and those not yet of registration age to the army. Yet that region has suffered severe famines year after year and repeatedly met with military defeats and setbacks, so that more than half the population has been lost; still, officials seek to round up the remaining able-bodied men, extending even to guest households. Even for those whom the ancients called surplus troops, the Precinct Master (Xiulüshi) in the Rites of Zhou still provided state gruel—how then can one bear to do this? In Guangdong and Guangxi there are recruited irregulars, which also resembles the Han-dynasty selective enlistments known as the "Brave and Daring" and the "[?]". Shiftless ruffians who know nothing of military registers or squad tallies bribe their way into the military [?] commands and collude to monopolize profits and commit abuses. Even when there are proposals to disband them, there is no [?]; and when they are dispatched to rush to the relief of an area, they cause turmoil wherever they go. This is meant to repel bandits—[but does it not rather] turn them into bandits themselves? As for these four practices, if we trace them back to their original institution, they were fundamentally sound, but they were ruined by later men who made slight concessions in the face of emergencies and then perpetuated those expedients as established precedents. Now, the collapse of a wall always begins with a crack, and the snapping of a sword always stems from a flaw. Today we see weapons rusted and blunt, battle-axes and halberds indiscriminately lenient, and swift horses turned back to haul dung, while people point to military affairs as inauspicious and refuse to discuss them. Theincipient signs are more subtle than a crack or a flaw, yet the resulting harm is greater than a ruined wall or a broken sword—how can we not be fearful?

punctuated: 國伍籍半折，丁壯阻消，物力方虛，杼軸困竭。則當倣《周禮》比居之法，詳覈所部，悉清勾之，而又官助其資斧，給其兵械。乃若免役而收其直，謂之更賦，是殆不可復矣。卽故直有所逋者，令得一切蠲貸可乎？入衛者近已議省，或三而省一，或二而省一，稍稍紓巳。但延綏遠走朔方，彫窭旣甚；寧夏屯牧河曲，困憊未甦。且毫□之涉，行者踣于道，至者羸于野，而復□□□□□，見人馬俱斃，主客胥窘矣。今山□□□□兵，而延、寧爲西陲重地，脫有緩□□□以應之？愚以爲盡免焉可也。古者國有游倅，軍有單，所以副其正也。今不得已而抽添之，無巳，當厚餉給。蓋羨卒旣搜，則糗糧皆畜，疇爲之副？宜於常賦之外，稍加優厚。而猶未給也，當廣屯種。遼地延袤殆千餘里，界山依水，可徼常居者，室家田作，復其繇稅，使流移漸集，生聚日繁。而又嚴逋逃之禁，重督
translation_en: …in the prefectures and principalities, the military registers are half depleted, able-bodied men are demoralized and dwindling, material resources are currently exhausted, and the looms stand empty. We ought to model ourselves on the method of neighborhood registration in the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli), thoroughly verify those under each jurisdiction, and clear out and draft them all, while the authorities assist with their traveling expenses and supply their weapons and armor. As for exempting them from service and collecting a payment instead—what was called the substitution tax (gengfu)—this surely cannot be restored. Even where past payments are in arrears, would it not be appropriate to order them entirely remitted and forgiven? As for the frontier troops rotating in to guard the capital, there have recently been deliberations to reduce their numbers—reducing either one in three or one in two—which has brought some slight relief. However, the Yansui troops march far from the northern regions and are already severely impoverished; the Ningxia troops garrison and herd in the bend of the Yellow River and have not yet recovered from their exhaustion. Moreover, during the trek of the slightest [?], those on the march collapse along the roads and those who arrive lie emaciated in the fields; and when on top of this […], we see both men and horses perishing, and host and guest troops alike reduced to distress. Now Shan-[…] troops, while Yansui and Ningxia are vital strategic places on the western frontier; should an emergency arise, [how could we] respond to it? In my humble opinion, it would be best to exempt them entirely. In antiquity, the state had unattached reserves (youcui) and the army had surplus men [?], which served to back up the regular forces. Now, having no choice, we levy additional men from the military households; if there is no alternative, we ought to provide them with generous rations and pay. For once the surplus men have been combed out, all must be fed with provisions—who then is left to support them as seconds? Beyond the regular stipends, we should grant them slightly more generous treatment. And if this is still insufficient, we ought to expand military agricultural colonies (tuntian). The territory of Liaodong stretches for nearly a thousand li, bounded by mountains and backed by rivers. Where permanent settlers can be invited [?], let them establish households and cultivate the fields, exempting them from corvée and taxes, so that displaced migrants gradually gather and the population grows daily more numerous. Furthermore, we should strictly enforce prohibitions against desertion, heavily supervise…

text:
邏司候徼支繚以譏闌出逸海及以賄脫
伍者庶幾行伍實而丁可無抽也古者藏
兵於民藏食於兵未嘗外索也今不得已
而用募曷若召土著高肇惠潮類多矯健
籍之行間使家與家相疇人與人相疇即
食其地習其將而將不得人不可也當選
將領汰其剝削而貪者張疑竊冒而詐者

者與無功同罰以此制募□□□亦足恃矣
若是者皆小補其罅隙者也而未盡也夫

punctuated:
邏，司候徼支繚，以譏闌出逸海及以賄脫伍者，庶幾行伍實而丁可無抽也。古者藏兵於民，藏食於兵，未嘗外索也。今不得已而用募，曷若召土著？高、肇、惠、潮類多矯健，籍之行間，使家與家相疇，人與人相疇，即食其地，習其將；而將不得人，不可也。當選將領，汰其剝削而貪者、張疑竊冒而詐者，誠得廉勇不二心之士，使□□□枹焉。而又嚴憲罰之令，毋令倖法，□□□□冠而薄譴；能討軍實者，與首□□□□□□逞者，與無功同罰。以此制募，□□□亦足恃矣。
若是者，皆小補其罅隙者也，而未盡也。夫軍能安制矜節而為國家用者，有數以至焉：曰制馭之有方也，不然，拊恤之愛及人深也，又不然，則簡習而訓練之也。語曰：「陷行亂陣，千人盡罰；覆軍殺將，萬人齊勇。」則必肅其營部，結其團伍，與之安，與之危，可以行，可以止，所謂用天下之用為用，制天
translation_en:
… patrols, and take charge of watchtowers, frontier outposts, and branching palisades to inspect and apprehend those who illicitly cross the border or flee by sea, as well as those who use bribes to abscond from the ranks. In this way, the military ranks may perhaps be kept full and there will be no need to conscript additional adult males.

In antiquity, soldiers were quartered among the populace, and provisions were stored within the military itself; there was never any need to seek them from outside. Now, since we have no choice but to use mercenaries, how could that compare to recruiting indigenous locals? In Gaozhou (高), Zhaoqing (肇), Huizhou (惠), and Chaozhou (潮), the people are mostly vigorous and strong. If we register them into the ranks, making household pair with household and man pair with man, they will live off their own local land and become accustomed to their own commanders. Yet if the commanders are not the right men, it will not do. We must select commanding officers, weeding out those who are exploitative and greedy, as well as those who spread false alarms, fraudulently claim merits, and act deceitfully. If we truly obtain incorruptible, brave, and single-minded men and have them [… hold the] drumstick, and furthermore strictly enforce the laws and penalties—never allowing anyone toluckily escape the law or [… receive] only a light reprimand, while rewarding those capable of attending to military realities on par with [taking enemy] heads [… and punishing those who recklessly] act on their own on par with having no merit—then if we regulate the mercenaries by these means, […] they too will be sufficient to rely upon.

Measures such as these, however, merely patch up small cracks and crevices; they do not get to the root of the matter. Now, for an army to be content under discipline, proud of its integrity, and ready to be of service to the state, there are fundamental principles by which this is achieved: namely, that there is a proper method for controlling and directing them; or else, that the affection shown in comforting and caring for them reaches deeply into the men; or else, that they are carefully selected, drilled, and trained.

As the saying goes: "When a line gives way and the battle formation is thrown into chaos, all thousand men are punished; to overthrow an enemy army and slay its commander, ten thousand men unite in valor." Thus, one must bring strict order to the camps and divisions, bind together the units and squads, share both safety and peril with them, and ensure they can advance or halt on command. punctuated: 下之制爲制，而奚恤乎軍寡？語曰：「畜恩不倦，以十取萬。」必使懼者得歡，貪者得豐，欲者得使，歸者得招。庶多同心之眾、必死之士，可合不可離，可用不可疲，而又奚恤乎軍寡？語曰：「習而後用，一以當百。」則圓而方之，生而死之，左而右之，聚則成卒，散則成列，延則若阿刃，嬰之者斷，□□若鋩銛，當之者碎，而又奚恤乎軍寡？□□□將少而能辦，將弱而能競，惟綏御□□□□乘服習，故雖匱乏困憊，一呼而□□，□□傷涉血而沰敵破虜矣。然此所□□□□之軍也，而內軍尤有可議焉。軍之利害，□國之名實。今三營之軍，名在官而實在家。在家者間役於私門，在官者或剝於衞尉。貧不能操一錢，食不能人二鬴，而牽露骨馬，環立轅門，負半石弓，載韜橐鞬，弛擔而赴營陳，一茇舍則負趨出市，絕不談兵。在籍則名選鋒，一簡稽則羸弱相參，曷稱全勇？夫
translation_en: … take the regulations of the world as one's regulations—so why worry that the troops are few? The saying goes: "Nurture grace tirelessly, and with ten you can take ten thousand." One must ensure that the fearful attain joy, the greedy attain abundance, those with desires are employed, and those who submit are welcomed. Thus there will be a multitude of one heart and warriors resolved to die, who can be united and cannot be divided, who can be used and cannot be exhausted—and why again worry that the troops are few? The saying goes: "Train them before using them, and one will match a hundred." Then whether turning them from round to square formations, leading them through life and death, or directing them left and right, when gathered they form squads, when dispersed they form ranks; extended, they are like the blade of a great sword that severs whatever touches it; […], they are like a sharp point that shatters whatever faces it—and why again worry that the troops are few? […] generals are able to manage despite being few, and able to contend despite being weak, only because they pacify and command […], and rely on training and familiarity. Therefore, even when lacking supplies and exhausted, at a single shout they […], [braving?] wounds and wading through blood to strike the enemy and crush the caitiffs. Yet what has been [discussed here concerns the frontier?] armies, whereas regarding the interior armies there is even more that calls for discussion. The advantages and disadvantages of the military [pertain to?] the nominal and the actual state of the realm. Today, the soldiers of the Three Training Divisions are nominally in official service, yet in reality they stay at home. Those at home are at times pressed into service by private households, while those in official service are sometimes fleeced by Guard Commanders. Poor, they cannot hold a single coin; for food, they cannot get two fu measures per man. Yet they lead gaunt, bony horses to stand in a ring around the camp gates, carrying half-shi bows and bearing bow-cases and quivers; they lay down their loads to go to the camp formations, and as soon as they halt to bivouac, they shoulder their gear and hurry out to the market, never speaking a word of military matters. On the registers they are called "chosen vanguard," yet upon a single inspection and muster, the emaciated and weak are mixed in among them—how can they be called completely brave? Now…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
賢王訓臣善學乎前代謹師乎當代蓋爲政必
先務學也酌諸古而準諸今治道其備乎成王
訓官若曰蒞官之道以緣法爲要以典學爲急
彼前代之政事可法可傳孰非聖君賢相所裁
成乎毋曰世代久遠而遂忽之也必學於入官
之初而猷訓之講習也豫議於臨事之際而權
度之審擇也精不愆於舊章也亦不泥於陳迹
也以古人之精蘊協吾心之化裁政斯不迷矣
然則慕古者可弗學哉以至當代之典常至精
===
至備孰非文武周公所講畫乎毋曰耳目習熟
而遂玩之也必仰制作之善而奉之以爲儀刑
覩品式之詳而率之以爲軌範彝憲不可易也
分義尤不可渝也以時王之道揆爲羣工之法
守政乃有恒矣然則生今者可弗學哉夫酌古
而亦不拂於今準今而亦不繆於古成王不惟
識治亦可謂知學者歟雖然制而用之存乎法
神而明之存乎人易曰通其變使民不倦非聖
人意也勢也若拘方以復古徇俗以從今則詭

分義尤不可渝也以時王之道揆爲羣工之法
守政乃有恒矣然則生今者可弗學哉夫酌古
而亦不拂於今準今而亦不繆於古成王不惟
識治亦可謂知學者歟雖然制而用之存乎法
神而明之存乎人易曰通其變使民不倦非聖
人意也勢也若拘方以復古狥俗以從今則詭
punctuated: 賢王訓臣，善學乎前代，謹師乎當代。蓋爲政必先務學也，酌諸古而準諸今，治道其備乎！成王訓官，若曰：蒞官之道，以緣法爲要，以典學爲急。彼前代之政事，可法可傳，孰非聖君賢相所裁成乎？毋曰世代久遠而遂忽之也，必學於入官之初，而猷訓之講習也豫；議於臨事之際，而權度之審擇也精。不愆於舊章也，亦不泥於陳迹也。以古人之精蘊，協吾心之化裁，政斯不迷矣。然則慕古者可弗學哉？以至當代之典常，至精至備，孰非文、武、周公所講畫乎？毋曰耳目習熟而遂玩之也，必仰制作之善，而奉之以爲儀刑；覩品式之詳，而率之以爲軌範。彝憲不可易也，分義尤不可渝也。以時王之道揆，爲羣工之法守，政乃有恒矣。然則生今者可弗學哉？夫酌古而亦不拂於今，準今而亦不繆於古，成王不惟識治，亦可謂知學者歟！雖然，制而用之存乎法，神而明之存乎人。《易》曰：「通其變，使民不倦。」非聖人意也，勢也。若拘方以復古，徇俗以從今，則詭
translation_en:
When the worthy king instructed his ministers, he urged them to learn well from former dynasties and carefully take the present dynasty as their teacher. For in administering government, one must first devote oneself to learning; by drawing upon antiquity and taking the present as one's standard, is the way of governance not made complete?

When King Cheng (Cheng Wang) instructed his officials, it was as if he said: In the way of assuming office, following the laws is essential, and devoting oneself to learning is urgent. Those governmental affairs of former dynasties that are worthy of emulation and transmission—which of them was not shaped and brought to completion by sage rulers and worthy ministers? Do not say that because those eras are distant in time, you may consequently neglect them. You must study them when first entering office, so that the discussion and practice of their plans and instructions are prepared in advance; and deliberate upon them when confronting affairs, so that the weighing and selection of standards are refined. Thus one neither errs against the old statutes, nor gets bogged down in stale traces. By harmonizing the subtle essence of the ancients with the adaptable judgment of one's own mind, governance will not go astray. This being so, how can those who admire antiquity fail to learn?

As for the constant institutions of the present dynasty, utmost in refinement and completeness—which of them was not deliberated and planned by King Wen, King Wu, and the Duke of Zhou (Zhou Gong)? Do not say that because your ears and eyes are familiar with them, you may consequently treat them lightly. You must look up to the excellence of their creations and uphold them as models; observe the detailed precision of their regulations and follow them as standards. The constant norms must not be altered, and the moral duties of one's station especially must not be transgressed. By taking the guiding principles of the reigning king as the laws to be guarded by all officials, governance will thereby have constancy. This being so, how can those born in the present age fail to learn?

Now, drawing upon antiquity without going against the present, and taking the present as standard without violating antiquity—King Cheng not only understood governance, but may also be said to have understood learning! Even so, instituting and employing them lies in the laws, whereas spiritually comprehending and illuminating them lies in the person. The Book of Changes (Yi) says: "comprehending its changes so that the people do not grow weary." This is not the arbitrary wish of the sage; it is the trend of circumstances. If one clings rigidly to fixed methods in order to restore antiquity, or yields to vulgar customs in order to follow the present, then [one falls into] perversity…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
連帥則責重藩垣作之屏而捍衞嚴作之翰而
保障固握千里之提封垂六服之成式厥功偉
矣滿假者居之鮮有不恃而自驕者彼則曰是
天子威澤所被也吾何有焉處亢思抑履盛思
危功愈大而心愈下蓋允懋裳華之德者也吾
見永綏厥祜而繁祉之穰穰以莫不增矣斯則
致恭以存位者夫豈有過謫哉自其在朝言之
志協泰交則情深晉接兕觥觩而爵斝行旨酒
柔而獻酬洽瞻一人之喜起荷五位之龍光厥
===
寵渥矣怙侈者承之鮮有不恃而自肆者彼則
曰是天子慈惠所流也吾何幸焉禮儀卒度笑
語卒獲寵愈厚而禮愈恭蓋善承湛露之恩者
也吾見聿懷多福而洪休之簡簡不求而至矣
斯固小心以獲上者寧不有譽處哉吁吾于桑
扈而知當時上下之交矣夫周王建國親侯恩
禮篤厚非下濟之光乎則臣之戢難匪敖要其
共上之自然而非矯也此天地交泰而和氣盈
宇內也然君不言已之盡禮而美臣之能敬謙

translation_en:
…as regional commanders (lianshuai), their responsibilities as bulwarks of the realm are weighty. Serving as screens, their defense is strict; serving as pillars, their protection is secure. Holding domains of a thousand li and handing down established models for the six regions of submission, their achievements are great indeed! When self-satisfied and arrogant men occupy such positions, few fail to presume upon them and grow proud; yet these lords say, "This is the reach of the Son of Heaven's majesty and grace; what part do we have in it?" Dwelling in exaltation, they think of restraint; treading in prosperity, they remain mindful of danger. The greater their merit, the humbler their hearts—truly they exert themselves in the virtue celebrated in "Glorious Are the Flowers" (Shanghua). Thus we see them forever secure in their blessings, with abundant felicity multiplying without end. Being those who carry utmost respect to preserve their positions, how could they incur any fault or blame?

Speaking of them when they are at court: their wills harmonize in the communion of the Peace (Tai) hexagram, and their feelings run deep in the audience of the Flourishing (Jin) hexagram. The curved rhinoceros-horn goblets are raised as the爵 (jue) and 斝 (jia) vessels circulate; the fine wine is mellow as toasts and pledges flow in harmony. Gazing upon the joyful rising of the One Man, and receiving the glorious favor of the royal throne, the grace bestowed upon them is rich indeed! When presumptuous and extravagant men receive such favor, few fail to rely upon it and become unrestrained; yet these lords say, "This is the outpouring of the Son of Heaven's benevolence and kindness; how fortunate we are!" Their ceremonial deportment is wholly according to measure, their laughter and speech wholly fitting; the deeper the favor, the more reverent their demeanor—truly they know how to receive the grace of "Heavy Lies the Dew" (Zhanlu). Thus we see them drawing to themselves manifold blessings, while vast and bountiful good fortune arrives unsought. Being those who exercise circumspection to win the confidence of their sovereign, how could they not enjoy fame and peace?

Ah! From the ode "Greenbeaks" (Sanghu), I understand the intercourse between superior and inferior in that era. When the King of Zhou established the feudatories and drew the feudal lords close, his grace and ritual courtesy were generous and deep—was this not the radiance of condescending to those below? Then the ministers' restraint [reading 難 as 儺] and lack of arrogance were, at bottom, the natural expression of their reverence for their sovereign, and nothing forced. This was heaven and earth communing in peace, filling the universe with harmoniousvitality. Yet the ruler does not speak of his own perfection in ritual courtesy, praising instead his ministers' capacity for reverence; within the radiance of humility…

…humility and radiance, admonition and caution reside therein. Is this not also the very air of an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers mutually perfecting one another?

"Broadly wise was he as a man; civil and martial was he as a ruler; he gave peace even unto August Heaven, and was able to make prosperous his descendants." [Classic of Poetry, "Yong" (雝)]

The sage king's virtue reached the utmost flourishing, and thereby he moved Heaven and enriched his descendants. Now, when flourishing virtue is brought forth in governance, none among the people fails to be at peace; moving Heaven by this means, how fitting it is that he should enrich his descendants! The ode "Yong" (雝) praises King Wen, meaning that Heaven establishes a ruler for the sake of the people, and shows favor to a ruler on account of his virtue; when virtue flourishes, the people are at peace, and his descendants also benefit from it—do I not depend upon my August Deceased Father? For the way of man is most subtle, and to illumine it with divine intelligence is not easy. My Deceased Father's wisdom was opened by Heaven: thus he was comprehensive and penetrating, discerning and knowing; like the shining down of the sun and moon, there was nothing dark or hidden that he did not illuminate—he was not merely the most spiritually endowed of the myriad creatures! The virtue of a ruler is most great, and to exercise it broadly and unceasingly is difficult. My Deceased Father's virtue was bestowed by Heaven: thus through civil virtue he was illustrious, and through martial virtue he was awe-inspiring; like yin…

傷也？然其所畏在齊，而與衛益之爲三，則□益堅，此其作俑乎？自齊而言，睢陽之交，固宋與我親矣，參何害也？然東諸侯互盛，而玆復合之爲一，則濫觴已甚，誰爲厲階乎？前有離盟者，自此而變，其趨將何所止？後有齊盟者，由玆而肇，其害有不可言。聖人欲盡洗刑歃之陋習，而遠追敬信之遺風也，敢不致其謹歟？噫！謹參盟，所以望不盟之意也，亦甚殷矣。雖然，聖人何心也？與時宜之者也。質文迭運，若循環然。質微而約之以法，盟可也，孔子意也；利巧勝而質以救之，不盟可也，亦文武意也。說者謂謹參盟爲變周制，愚謂雖復古道，亦憲章文武之心云。

translation_en:
…what harm would there be? Yet what they feared was Qi, and by adding Wei to make three, the [alliance?] grew even firmer—was this not the original instigation? Speaking from the standpoint of Qi, in the relations at Suiyang, Song and we were already close; what harm was there in a tripartite alliance? Yet as the eastern feudal lords vied in power, now combining them once more into one meant the overflowing source had already gone too far—who was the stepping-stone to this disorder? Previously there were bilateral covenants (limeng), which changed from this point on—where would their tendency stop? Later there were general covenants (qimeng), which originated from this—their harm is beyond words. Since the Sage wished to completely wash away the base custom of slaughtering victims and smearing blood on the lips, and to reach far back to the remaining ethos of reverence and trustworthiness, how could he dare not exercise the utmost caution? Alas! Being cautious about tripartite covenants was the very means by which he hoped for the ideal of making no covenants at all, and his intent was most earnest indeed. Even so, what was in the Sage's mind? It was simply to adapt appropriately to the times. Substance and refinement alternate like a cycle. When substance declines and one binds people by rules, making covenants is permissible—such was the intent of Confucius. When calculation and artifice prevail and one rescues the situation with substance, making no covenants is permissible—and this too was the intent of Kings Wen and Wu. Commentators say that being cautious about tripartite covenants was altering the institutions of Zhou; in my humble view, even if it was restoring the ancient Way, it was also the mind that modeled itself on Kings Wen and Wu.

"The men of Qi attacked the Mountain Rong" [thirtieth year of Duke Zhuang]; "In the sixth month, the Marquis of Qi came to present the spoils of the Rong" [thirty-first year of Duke Zhuang]; "In spring, in the King's first month, the Duke met the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, and the Earl of Cao to make an incursion into Cai; Cai collapsed, whereupon they attacked Chu and halted at Xing"; "They made a covenant at Shaoling" [both in the fourth year of Duke Xi].

《春秋》志覇兵，有譏其畧遠者，有美其服遠者。此見齊桓北伐山戎、南伐楚，而失得不相掩矣。聖人之意，蓋以爲先王御天下，務治內以強本，而外夷非所急也。故修德而弗征，即薄征而弗甚，要在柔服之而止爾。
山戎處要荒之服而病燕，豈若《詩》之歌「孔熾」乎？乃桓之北伐也，提境內之单師，越險道以臨孤竹，不覿德而覿威焉。當時戎方驍喙，遂快心于龜蒙之獻矣。詎知涉不毛之地以罷民，即盡戎人而俘之，竟何益哉！噫！吾觀管仲軌里連鄉之法，且嘉其無煩役而謹內治也；乃今勤兵畧遠如是，故《春秋》稱「人」以譏之。
楚負江漢之強而猾夏，奚啻《詩》之詠獫狁乎？乃桓之南伐也，合諸侯之大衆，次陘亭以問包茅，
translation_en:
Associate Examiner and Historiographer of the Hanlin Academy Liu comments: "It fully develops the meaning of governing the interior and mollifying distant peoples; a piece of writing with real relevance."
Associate Examiner and Historiographer of the Hanlin Academy Sheng comments: "Strict, orderly, elegant, and vigorous; an excellent exposition of the classic. Selected for inclusion."
Examiner and Academician Reader-in-Waiting Yu comments: "Strict in structure and polished in phrasing."
Examiner and Grand Secretary Shen comments: "Neat, clean, and well-proportioned."
When the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) records the military expeditions of the hegemons, in some cases it criticizes them for seizing distant lands, and in others it praises them for bringing distant peoples to submission. From this we see how Duke Huan of Qi attacked the Mountain Rong in the north and attacked Chu in the south, and how his failures and successes do not obscure one another. The intention of the Sage was doubtless that when the former kings ruled the world, they devoted themselves to governing the interior in order to strengthen the root, whereas the outer barbarians were not an urgent priority. Thus they cultivated virtue and did not launch punitive expeditions, or if they did launch minor expeditions, they did not press them to extremes—the essential point was simply to mollify and bring them to submission, and nothing more.
The Mountain Rong dwelt in the outer zones of constraint and the wilds and harassed Yan; how could this be compared to the "fiercely blazing" threat sung of in the Odes (Shi)? Yet in Duke Huan's northern expedition, he led a lone army from within his borders and crossed treacherous roads to march upon Guzhu, displaying not virtue, but military might. At the time, the Rong were fierce and rapacious, and so he gratified his desires with the presentation of spoils beneath Mount Guimeng. How could he know that in crossing barren lands and exhausting the people, even if he captured every last one of the Rong, what benefit would it ultimately bring? Alas! When I examine Guan Zhong's system of organizing neighborhoods and linking districts, I admire how he avoided burdensome corvée labor and attended carefully to internal governance; yet now he mobilized troops to seize distant lands like this, and therefore the Spring and Autumn Annals refers to him merely as a "man" of Qi in order to criticize him.
Chu relied on the strength of the Yangzi and Han rivers to throw the central states into disorder—how was this any less than the Xianyun sung of in the Odes? Yet in Duke Huan's southern expedition, he united the great host of the feudal lords and halted at Xingting to call Chu to account for the tribute of wrapped three-ribbed rushes, …

text:
不鬭力而鬭義焉當時楚兵未交遂斂手于召
陵之盟矣借令豔折馘之功以輕敵卽環楚城
而攻之能必勝哉噫吾觀敬仲牢山蔽海之謀
且恐其有侈心而荒內治也乃今慎兵服遠如
是故春秋書次以美之抑此卑卑霸事耳無庸
論已後之王者若用武而空幕南之庭固宜海
內虛耗至于朝呼韓臣昆彌而天下亦敝何歟

不鬭力而鬭義焉。當時楚兵未交，遂斂手于召陵之盟矣。借令豔折馘之功以輕敵，卽環楚城而攻之，能必勝哉？噫！吾觀敬仲牢山蔽海之謀，且恐其有侈心而荒內治也；乃今慎兵服遠如是，故《春秋》書「次」以美之。抑此卑卑霸事耳，無庸論已。後之王者，若用武而空幕南之庭，固宜海內虛耗；至于朝呼韓、臣昆彌，而天下亦敝，何歟？蓋國之所恃以安者，內治而已。恃四夷之柔服，而忘備于衣袽，則外寧固內憂之所以萌也。《書》言來王之效，而必戒夫怠荒，請以此足強本治內之意。

禮記

合情飾貌者，禮樂之事也。禮義立，則貴賤等矣；樂文同，則上下和矣。

同考試官主事曹批：理到之文，無用費詞，而題旨躍然，宜錄以式。
同考試官編修史批：發禮樂救弊之說，詞簡而意盡。
translation_en:
…he did not contend through force, but contended through righteousness. At that time, before the forces of Chu had even crossed blades, they folded their hands and submitted at the covenant of Shaoling. Suppose he had coveted the glory of taking severed ears and lightly engaged the enemy—even if he had surrounded the cities of Chu and besieged them, could he have been certain of victory? Alas! When I observe Jingzhong's [Guan Zhong's] plans for monopolizing the mountains and enclosing the seas, I even fear that he harbored an extravagant heart and neglected internal governance; yet now, he was so cautious with the military in subduing distant peoples, and therefore the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) recorded his "halting" (ci) in order to praise him. Yet these are merely the lowly affairs of hegemons, not worth discussing further. As for later rulers, if one used military force to empty the royal court south of the desert, it was only natural that the realm within the seas was exhausted; yet when it came to bringing Huhanye to court and making the Kunmi a subject, the empire was also worn out—why was this? It is because what a state relies upon for security is internal governance and nothing more. If one relies on the compliant submission of the four border tribes and forgets the precaution of rags for caulking leaks, then external peace is surely the very thing from which internal worries sprout. The Book of Documents (Shu) speaks of the efficacy of foreign rulers coming to pay homage, yet insists on warning against indolence and neglect; I beg to use this to complete the meaning of strengthening the root and governing the interior.

Record of Rites (Liji)

"To harmonize the feelings and adorn the outward appearance is the business of rites and music. When the principles of ritual are established, the noble and the base are differentiated according to rank; when the patterns of music are shared in common, superiors and inferiors are brought into harmony."

Associate Examiner, Secretary (zhushi) Cao comments: An essay that arrives at the true principle. Without wasting words, the import of the topic leaps vividly to life; it should be recorded as a model.
Associate Examiner, Historiographer (bianxiu) Shi comments: It brings forth the theory of how rites and music remedy defects; the words are concise, yet the meaning is fully expressed.

text:
考試官侍讀學士秦批詞醇意徹
考試官大學士申批簡當
論禮樂相資之事而因著其功焉盖禮樂交相
爲用則可以無弊矣其功豈小補哉且先王之
制禮樂非能必其致用之不偏而惟恃吾救弊
之有道何以言之聯天下之好者情也禮勝而
離情則暌矣於焉合之以孚其恩意之交律天
下之觀者貌也樂勝而流貌則褻矣於焉飾之
以謹其威儀之則此豈得諸禮樂之外哉一序
===
一和不可以偏廢而修內修外乃所以相資則
禮樂之事歸焉耳誠知禮之有資於樂也用之
以飾貌而義立焉則莊敬品節體統得之以相
維而貴以率賤賤以承貴自肅然有等矣貌飾
而樂不患於流玆非禮之功乎知樂之有資於
禮也用之以合情而文同焉則和順周流意氣
得之以相洽而上之愛下下之親上自藹然咸
和矣情合而禮不患於離玆非樂之功乎即以
禮樂之道還救禮樂之偏先王制作所以垂之

論禮樂相資之事，而因著其功焉。盖禮樂交相爲用，則可以無弊矣，其功豈小補哉？且先王之制禮樂，非能必其致用之不偏，而惟恃吾救弊之有道。何以言之？聯天下之好者，情也；禮勝而離，情則暌矣，於焉合之，以孚其恩意之交。律天下之觀者，貌也；樂勝而流，貌則褻矣，於焉飾之，以謹其威儀之則。此豈得諸禮樂之外哉？一序一和，不可以偏廢，而修內修外，乃所以相資，則禮樂之事歸焉耳。誠知禮之有資於樂也，用之以飾貌而義立焉，則莊敬品節，體統得之以相維，而貴以率賤，賤以承貴，自肅然有等矣。貌飾而樂不患於流，玆非禮之功乎？知樂之有資於禮也，用之以合情而文同焉，則和順周流，意氣得之以相洽，而上之愛下，下之親上，自藹然咸和矣。情合而禮不患於離，玆非樂之功乎？即以禮樂之道，還救禮樂之偏，先王制作所以垂之
translation_en:
Examiner Academician Reader-in-waiting Qin 秦 comments: Pure in diction and thorough in meaning.
Examiner Grand Secretary Shen 申 comments: Concise and apt.

[The passage] discusses the task of how rites and music complement one another, and thereby sets forth their efficacy. Indeed, when rites and music serve one another in turn, they can be free from defects; is their efficacy merely a minor help?

Moreover, when the Former Kings instituted rites and music, it was not that they could guarantee their application would be free from one-sidedness; rather, they relied solely on having a way to remedy their defects. How may we explain this? What binds together the goodwill of the world is sentiment (qing); when rites prevail excessively and cause estrangement, sentiments become alienated, and thereupon one unites them so as to inspire mutual trust in grace and goodwill. What regulates the deportment seen by the world is outward demeanor (mao); when music prevails excessively and leads to dissipation, demeanor becomes irreverent, and thereupon one adorns it so as to be heedful of the rules of dignified bearing. How could this be obtained outside of rites and music? Order on the one hand and harmony on the other cannot be emphasized at the expense of either, and cultivating the inner and cultivating the outer are precisely how they complement one another—thus this belongs to the business of rites and music alone.

Truly knowing that rites are of assistance to music, when one employs them to adorn demeanor and the righteous principles of rites are established therein, then through solemn reverence and graded regulation the hierarchical system is maintained, so that the noble lead the base and the base serve the noble, naturally standing in reverent order by rank. When demeanor is adorned and music does not suffer from dissipation, is this not the efficacy of rites? Knowing that music is of assistance to rites, when one employs it to unite sentiments and the patterns of music are shared in common therein, then through harmonious compliance and all-pervading flow dispositions come to blend with one another, so that superiors love inferiors and inferiors feel affection for superiors, naturally becoming altogether genial and harmonious. When sentiments are united and rites do not suffer from estrangement, is this not the efficacy of music? By using the very Way of rites and music to turn back and remedy the one-sidedness of rites and music, the reason the institutions of the Former Kings could be handed down…

君子敬身以及親，惟立於無過而已。夫言動出於身者也，無過則能敬矣，而成親不在玆乎？夫子告哀公若曰：君子受其身於吾親，而託其身於民上，過言過動，百姓何觀焉？敢不敬歟！是以
translation_en:
… have been handed down without defect is because of this. Moreover, I have observed this in the Book of Changes (Yi): rites were instituted in the hexagram Treading (Lü), and music was created in the hexagram Enthusiasm (Yu). Yet in speaking of Treading, it says, "Treading is harmonious and reaches the ultimate"; and the good fortune of the second yin line of Enthusiasm is obtained through centrality and correctness. From this it can be seen that the principles of harmony and order inherently penetrate both rites and music, without either one prevailing at the expense of the other. Even so, the subtlety of equilibrium and harmony is complete within the single mind; if one is able to govern the mind, then one can govern rites and music.

"The gentleman's words do not go beyond proper phrasing, and his actions do not go beyond proper rules; thus the common people are reverent and respectful without being commanded. When it is like this, he is able to respect his own person; being able to respect his own person, he is able to bring fulfillment to his parents."

Comment by Associate Examiner and Secretary Cao: Pure, elegant, and poised with deep reserve; when recited, it rings with the resonant sound of metal and jade. This is someone deeply versed in the Classic of Rites.
Comment by Associate Examiner and Historiographer Shi: The structure and style are grave and dignified, the diction and reasoning refined and pure; it may serve as a model.
Comment by Examiner and Academician Reader-in-Waiting Qin: Classical and substantial, without superficiality.
Comment by Examiner and Grand Secretary Shen: Coherent and fluent.

For the gentleman to respect his own person and thereby extend that to his parents lies simply in establishing himself where he is free from transgression. Now, words and actions issue from one's person; if they are free from transgression, then one is able to respect oneself, and does not bringing fulfillment to one's parents lie right here? Master Confucius addressed Duke Ai as if to say: The gentleman receives his body from his parents and entrusts his person to a position above the common people. If there are transgressive words or transgressive actions, what example would the hundred surnames have to look upon? How could he dare not be reverent! Therefore, …

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
君子不苟言也言必求其成文而不過於辭不
苟動也動必求其成法而不過於則為律為度
允協百姓之心而祗若者無煩令也承聽承順
咸仰君子之德而欽服者有同情也夫如是斯
敬身之事盡矣而成親之道存焉蓋言動修於
上則在我臨御之身旣處於寡尤寡悔矣而身
之所自出者亦將貽以令名未有不虧其體而
顧辱其親者也敬恭協於下則斯民視效之身
旣示以可畏可象矣而身之所篤生者亦將永
===
有令聞所謂不失其身而能事其親者也然則
敬身者不必外言動求之而成親者亦豈外敬
身得之乎故曰敬身為大也雖然敬豈一日之
積哉戰戰兢兢臨深履薄一出言舉足而不忘
至於全歸而後為無忝斯亦難矣魯君蓋未嘗
知勞未甞知懼欲其敬身成親得乎故知夫子
有為言之也
第貳塲
論

有爲言之也
第貳場
論
punctuated:
君子不苟言也，言必求其成文，而不過於辭；不苟動也，動必求其成法，而不過於則。為律為度，允協百姓之心，而祗若者無煩令也；承聽承順，咸仰君子之德，而欽服者有同情也。夫如是，斯敬身之事盡矣，而成親之道存焉。蓋言動修於上，則在我臨御之身，旣處於寡尤寡悔矣，而身之所自出者，亦將貽以令名，未有不虧其體而顧辱其親者也。敬恭協於下，則斯民視效之身，旣示以可畏可象矣，而身之所篤生者，亦將永有令聞，所謂不失其身而能事其親者也。然則敬身者，不必外言動求之；而成親者，亦豈外敬身得之乎？故曰：「敬身為大」也。雖然，敬豈一日之積哉？戰戰兢兢，臨深履薄，一出言舉足而不忘，至於全歸，而後為無忝，斯亦難矣。魯君蓋未嘗知勞，未甞知懼，欲其敬身成親，得乎？故知夫子有為言之也。
第貳塲
論
translation_en:
… the gentleman does not speak carelessly; in speaking, he must seek for his words to form a pattern and not err in expression. He does not act carelessly; in acting, he must seek for his conduct to form a model and not err against the standard. Serving as a law and a measure, he truly harmonizes with the hearts of the hundred surnames, so that those who reverently comply require no troublesome orders; listening and obeying, all look up to the virtue of the gentleman, and those who admire and submit share the same feelings. Being thus, the task of revering one's own person is fulfilled, and the way of bringing honor to one's parents is preserved therein. For when speech and action are cultivated above, one's own person that governs already abides in a state of few faults and few regrets, and those from whom one's person originated will also be bequeathed a good name—there has never been one who kept his body unimpaired and yet disgraced his parents. When reverence and respect are harmonized below, the person whom the people look to and imitate has already shown himself worthy of awe and emulation, and those who gave birth to his person will also eternally possess a good reputation—this is what is meant by "not losing one's own person and thereby being able to serve one's parents." This being so, he who reveres his own person need not seek it outside of speech and action; and how could he who brings honor to his parents attain it outside of revering his own person? Therefore it is said: "Revering one's own person is the greatest thing." Even so, how could reverence be the accumulation of a single day? Trembling with apprehension, as if on the brink of a deep abyss or treading on thin ice, never forgetting in a single word spoken or a single step taken, until one returns whole at the end—only then is one free from shame, and this too is difficult! The ruler of Lu had never known toil and had never known fear; to wish for him to revere his own person and bring honor to his parents—was that possible? Thus we know that the Master spoke these words with a specific purpose in mind.

Plan for the Enduring Longevity of the Ancestral Altars and the Living People

Comment by Associate Examiner Compiler Liu: Whether the ruler's virtue is cultivated or not is what determines the order or neglect of the realm. Assisting and nurturing the ruler's virtue must rely on upright men; it depends only on how the ruler settles his plan and whether he keeps them close or at a distance. Few of the discourses caught sight of the essential point; this essay alone expresses impassioned and incisive ideas in extraordinary, magnificent language. Its author must be one who holds fast to rectitude, desires to be loyal, and sets his ambition on rectifying and assisting the sovereign—we may rejoice at having found the right man!

Comment by Associate Examiner Compiler Sheng: Drawing close to upright men in order to assist one's virtue is the supreme plan for a ruler, and candidates taking up their brushes are all able to say so; yet when it comes to why virtue absolutely cannot lack assistance and why upright men absolutely cannot be kept from closeness, their ideas fail to reach it. This piece alone is able, in vast, profound, and earnest words, to briskly set forth and minutely analyze the matter. Its author must be one who maintains himself with rectitude and constantly harbors loyal sincerity; it should be recorded as a model for the many scholars.

Comment by Examiner Academician Reader-in-Waiting Yu: It develops the meaning of assisting and nurturing the ruler's virtue clearly and exhaustively, while its diction is grand and vigorous, its learning and insight deep and vast, and counsels of loyal sincerity appear graciously beyond the words themselves. This is not something a person of shallow learning could attain; he truly deserves to be called a scholar of the realm, and it is fitting that he be recommended for first place.

Comment by Examiner Grand Secretary Shen: In discussing how the ruler ought to draw close to upright men, the exposition is thorough and complete, and at the end he further sets forth sincere devotion and offers admonition, fully revealing his loyal dedication. He deserves to crown the many scholars.

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
兆庶垂鴻業於罔極豈其恣心佚德而能晏然
託於巍巍之上乎蓋人主之身與宗社生靈為
命而不可一日肆也正人君子與人主共宗社
生靈之命而不可一日去也人主日親正人以
成其德而後其身安身安則萬世安故善置其
身者乃所謂善置天下者也程子言宗社生靈
長久之計惟在輔養上德而歸之不離正人蓋
古之大臣所以願忠於君者如此請為之明其
意人主之治天下未有計不先定而能臻於至
===
平者也農人終歲勤動望不過百畝封君之富
居材不過千章然而智盡能索不遺餘慮者何
也其自為計審也故曰一歲之計樹穀數歲之
計樹木而況人主為宗社生靈計將安出哉其
身愈貴者其神愈勞其責彌重者其慮彌遠以
奉宗廟則累世之德澤存焉然而九鼎在陳三
恪在列以此思憂憂無不至矣以承社稷則百
神之靈爽在焉然而有勝國之屋有故都之黍
以此思懼懼無不至矣以臨億兆生靈則戴髮

兆庶，垂鴻業於罔極，豈其恣心佚德，而能晏然託於巍巍之上乎？蓋人主之身，與宗社生靈為命，而不可一日肆也；正人君子，與人主共宗社生靈之命，而不可一日去也。人主日親正人以成其德，而後其身安，身安則萬世安。故善置其身者，乃所謂善置天下者也。程子言：「宗社生靈長久之計，惟在輔養上德。」而歸之不離正人，蓋古之大臣所以願忠於君者如此，請為之明其意。
人主之治天下，未有計不先定而能臻於至平者也。農人終歲勤動，望不過百畝；封君之富，居材不過千章。然而智盡能索，不遺餘慮者，何也？其自為計審也。故曰：「一歲之計樹穀，數歲之計樹木。」而況人主為宗社生靈計，將安出哉？其身愈貴者其神愈勞，其責彌重者其慮彌遠。以奉宗廟，則累世之德澤存焉；然而九鼎在陳，三恪在列，以此思憂，憂無不至矣。以承社稷，則百神之靈爽在焉；然而有勝國之屋，有故都之黍，以此思懼，懼無不至矣。以臨億兆生靈，則戴髮…
translation_en:
…the millions of common people, and pass down the great enterprise without end—how could he indulge his heart and neglect his virtue, and yet peacefully entrust himself to the lofty height above? Indeed, the person of the ruler is bound to the fate of the ancestral temple, the altars of soil and grain, and the living people, and thus he cannot be self-indulgent for a single day; upright men and gentlemen share with the ruler the fate of the ancestral temple, the altars of soil and grain, and the living people, and thus they cannot be dispensed with for a single day. Only when the ruler daily draws close to upright men to perfect his virtue is his person secure, and when his person is secure, then the ten thousand generations are secure. Therefore, one who knows how to properly situate his own person is what is meant by one who knows how to properly situate the empire. Master Cheng (Chengzi) said: "The long-term plan for the ancestral temple, the altars of soil and grain, and the living people lies solely in assisting and nourishing the sovereign's virtue," and he concluded this with never departing from upright men. Such was the way the great ministers of antiquity wished to be loyal to their lord; allow me to elucidate its meaning.

In a ruler's governance of the empire, it has never happened that he could attain supreme peace without his plan first being settled. A farmer toils all year long, yet his expectation does not exceed a hundred mu of land; a titled lord in his wealth stores timber not exceeding a thousand great logs. Yet they exhaust their wisdom and deplete their abilities, sparing no remaining thought—why is this? Because the plans they make for themselves are thorough. Thus it is said: "For a one-year plan, plant grain; for a multi-year plan, plant trees." How much more so when the ruler makes plans for the ancestral temple, the altars of soil and grain, and the living people—from where shall those plans proceed? The more noble one's person, the more taxed one's spirit; the heavier one's responsibility, the more far-reaching one's concerns. In serving the ancestral temple, the accumulated virtue and beneficence of successive generations abide there; yet the Nine Tripods are on display and the Three Revered Guests (descendants of former dynasties) stand in the ranks—if by this one ponders sorrow, there is no sorrow to which one will not arrive. In succeeding to the altars of soil and grain, the numinous presence of the hundred spirits abides there; yet there are the roofed altars of vanquished states and the millet of former capitals—if by this one ponders fear, there is no fear to which one will not arrive. In presiding over the hundreds of millions of living people, those with hair on their heads…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
人齒之倫爭犇走焉然而有朽索之虞有覆舟
之喻以此思危危無不至矣人主立於可憂可
懼之地而履至危之機將以投之至安而易之
以其所可樂使世世長久而無患不已難乎夫
智籠羣愚有時而詘力并衆強有時而摧整齊
一切之法綢繆其文章有時而玩則人主雖日
營營焉勞其心於天下然計在眉睫而或蔽於
丘山計在千里而或遺於几席非所以建萬世
之策奠宗社生靈於長久者也蓋宗社生靈之
===
所倚賴者曰人主而人主所與共宗社生靈者
曰正人人主務為長久之計也則惟日親正人
而已矣且人主之心不能使之無所繫而恒欲
其繫之於正也人主之身不患其無所託而恒
慮其託之於危也託於佞幸而以淫哇柔曼蠱
其心則身危託於儇巧而以游敖弋獵蕩其心
則身危託於叨憤而以凶殘掊克中其心則身
危託於險壬而以猜忌狠愎亂其心則身危正
人者有詔其媺而已矣有弼其違而已矣能為

人昔嘗詔其嬾而已矣有弼其違而已矣能爲

translation_en: …and possesses teeth [?] competes to hasten to his service; yet there is the peril of driving with rotten reins and the metaphor of the overturned boat. Reflecting on danger in this light, there is no limit to the danger. When a ruler stands in a position that gives cause for sorrow and fear, and treads upon the triggers of utmost peril, yet wishes to cast them into utmost safety and exchange them for what brings joy, ensuring longevity for generation after generation without calamity—is this not moeilijk indeed? Now, using cleverness to ensnare the foolish masses will at times fall short; using force to subdue the strong multitude will at times be broken; and using uniform laws to impose order, tightly weaving their statutory provisions, will at times be treated with contempt. Thus, although a ruler may busily toil in mind over the realm day after day, if his calculations focus on what is right before his eyes while perhaps being blinded to mountains, or if his calculations reach a thousand li away while perhaps overlooking what is right at his sitting mat, this is not the way to establish a plan for ten thousand generations or to settle the ancestral temples, the altars of soil and grain, and the living people in lasting security. For what the ancestral temples, the altars, and the people rely upon is called the ruler, and those with whom the ruler shares the care of the ancestral temples, the altars, and the people are called upright men. If the ruler is bent on making plans for lasting security, he need only draw close to upright men day by day, and nothing more. Moreover, the ruler's mind cannot be made to have nothing to which it attaches itself, yet one always desires that it attach itself to what is upright; the ruler's person does not suffer from having nothing upon which to entrust itself, yet one is always concerned lest it entrust itself to what is perilous. If he entrusts himself to sycophants and favorites, who seduce his mind with licentious tunes and soft, alluring charms, then his person is in peril; if he entrusts himself to nimble opportunists, who dissipate his mind with roaming, leisure, and hunting, then his person is in peril; if he entrusts himself to the greedy and resentful [?], who strike a chord in his mind with cruelty and extortion, then his person is in peril; if he entrusts himself to the treacherous and artful, who throw his mind into confusion with suspicion, ruthlessness, and obstinacy, then his person is in peril. As for upright men, they simply proclaim what is admirable to him, and nothing more; they simply correct his transgressions, and nothing more. They are capable of being…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
戇不能爲諂能爲拂不能爲順誠心質行見以
爲遲鈍迂闊而積之則有所感動讜論直言驟
以爲草野倨侮而久之則有所開發卽不幸人
主有溢志慆心國家有失道之敗而折其萌芽
苴其罅漏彌縫而匡救之非斯人莫與也是以
古之聖王側席而求推心而任師保疑丞非虛
位也而知綴衣虎賁之恤庶府百司非乏員也
而嚴侍御攜僕之選墳典丘索非闕於陳而重
工師矇瞍之規筍虡鞀鐸非解於懸而備諫諍
===
糾繩之職盤盂戶牖非不足於觀省而立書過
授環之史自昧爽而日昃自三朝而六寢自考
政而卽安出入之與俱動息之與游而不肯以
一日離者何也爲宗社生靈計長久當如是也
蓋發而後禁則有滔天燎原之虞密於此而疎
於彼則有一暴十寒之患賢者規之不肖者間
之則有一齊衆楚之憂人主惟日親正人聞正
言見正事目不闚瑰異之好耳不入陵亂之聲
志不動慆淫之感然後其心一繫之於正而其
