translation_en: … blunt, and cannot be flattering; they can be oppositional, and cannot be compliant. Their sincere hearts and plain conduct may appear slow-witted and impractical at first sight, yet as these accumulate they move the ruler's heart; their honest counsel and forthright words may suddenly seem rustic and insolent, yet over time they enlighten his mind. Even if, unfortunately, the ruler harbors extravagant ambitions or an indulgent heart, or the state suffers a failure from losing the Way, to nip the buds in the sprout, mend the cracks and leaks, and patch up and rectify the situation—without such men, there is no one with whom to accomplish this. Therefore, the sage kings of antiquity waited in humble anticipation to seek them out, and placed their full confidence in employing them. It was not that the posts of Preceptor, Guardian, Coadjutor, and Assistant were empty titles, yet the kings were mindful of the care taken in choosing the keepers of the robes and the palace guards; it was not that the various storehouses and hundred offices lacked personnel, yet they were strict in selecting close attendants and personal grooms; it was not that the Classic of the Three Sovereigns, the Classic of the Five Emperors, the Eight Trigrams, and the Nine Provinces failed to be set forth before them, yet they valued the admonitions of the blind musicians; it was not that the bell-frames, hand-drums, and clapper-bells were taken down from their stands, yet they fully staffed the offices of remonstrance and rectification; it was not that inscriptions on basins, bowls, doors, and windows were insufficient for visual self-examination, yet they established scribes to record faults and present the jade ring of regulation. From the break of dawn until the sun inclined to the west, from the three outer courts to the six inner chambers, from examining governance to retiring for rest, going out and coming in together with them, moving and resting in their company, and refusing to be separated from them for even a single day—why was this? Because in planning for the long-term endurance of the ancestral temple, the altars of soil and grain, and the living people, it ought to be thus. For if one forbids something only after it has broken out, there is the danger of a flood swelling to heaven or a fire blazing across the plain; if one is attentive here yet neglectful there, there is the trouble of one day of warmth followed by ten days of cold; if the worthy admonish the ruler while the unworthy sow discord between them, there is the worry of a single man of Qi amidst a multitude of men from Chu. Only when the ruler daily draws close to upright men, hears upright words, and sees upright deeds—his eyes not peering at curiosities and strange delights, his ears not admitting disorderly and chaotic sounds, and his will not stirred by indolent and licentious impulses—is his mind wholly bound to what is upright, and his…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
身益託之於安是故澄然穆然德修於淵蜎濩
濩之中而政行於拱揖指麾之上化隆澤洽升
聞於天而固結於民於以承九廟奉六親崇蘊
穹窿之宗百世而不遷至孝也社稷有奉鬼神
福饗垂之世世與天無極至明也以幸天下以
育羣生百姓欣然戴之願長以為君師至仁也
大業光乎來裔休聲浹乎于茲不下莞簟而萬
世久長之慶集矣夫人主何以得此哉善建者
不拔彼所謂置其身於至安而後能置天下者
===
也季世之主履大寶乘昌運崇滿之勢易極而
輔養之義闕如正者不親親者不正於是旒黈
之外若隔九閽焉天人之怨交積而大業墜矣
則豈非置身殊路而安危異效哉昔者成王蓋
冲厭而聽天下公旦為輔選天下之端士博聞
有道術者與之游處前後左右罔匪正人故周
道以醲卜世卜年皆過其曆秦之二世託於宵
人之手而繆為之說曰天子所以貴者但以聞
聲羣臣莫得見焉於是德澤無一有而怨毒盈

translation_en:
…person is ever more firmly grounded in security. Therefore, in pure tranquility and solemn serenity, his virtue is cultivated amidst deep stillness and secluded quietude, while his governance is carried out through composed bows and effortless command from above. When moral transformation flourishes and beneficent grace is all-pervading, his virtue ascends to be heard by Heaven and binds the hearts of the people fast. Thereby to succeed to the nine ancestral temples, to honor the six kindred relations, and to exalt the lofty ancestral lineage so that it remains unmoved for a hundred generations—this is the utmost filial piety. For the altars of soil and grain to receive their sacrifices, and for the spirits and gods to enjoy their offerings and bestow blessings, handing this down from generation to generation as boundless as Heaven—this is the utmost enlightenment. To bring good fortune to the realm and nurture all living things, so that the common people joyfully revere him and wish forever to take him as their ruler and teacher—this is the utmost benevolence. The great enterprise shines upon future descendants, and fine reputation permeates the present; without his even stepping down from his woven reed and bamboo mats, the blessings of ten thousand generations of enduring longevity are gathered together. Now, how does a ruler attain this? "What is well planted cannot be uprooted." This is what was meant by placing one's own person in supreme security, and only thereafter being able to place the whole realm in security.

Rulers of degenerate ages occupy the great treasure of the throne and ride upon prosperous fortunes; their exalted and full position easily reaches an extreme, while the principle of assisting and nurturing the sovereign's virtue is altogether lacking. Those who are upright are not kept close, and those who are kept close are not upright; consequently, beyond the垂 pendants of his crown and the silk earplugs, he is as if cut off by the nine gates of Heaven. The resentment of Heaven and humanity accumulates together, and the great enterprise falls to ruin. Is this not because placing one's person on different paths yields opposite outcomes of security and peril? In antiquity, King Cheng was still in his tender youth [?] when he governed the realm. Duke Dan of Zhou acted as his coadjutor, selecting upright gentlemen of the world—men of broad learning and possession of the Way and its arts—to associate and dwell with him. Ahead and behind, to the left and right, there was none who was not an upright man. Therefore, the Way of Zhou grew rich and deep, and the divined generations and divined years both surpassed their predicted span. The Second Emperor of Qin entrusted himself to the hands of a petty man, who craftily fabricated a theory for him, saying: "The reason the Son of Heaven is noble is that people only hear his voice, and none of the ministers may see his face." Thereupon, not a single shred of virtuous grace existed, while resentment and bitterness filled…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
於世一夫作難而七廟隳矣夫周之所以久長
者其計得也秦之所以亟絕者其計失也後之
君臣覩周之已事鑒秦之覆轍無亦兢兢於輔
養之術哉嗟乎世道之趨猶江河之不可返也
自堂陛森嚴尊卑闊絕人主之不能朝夕而臨
羣臣也久矣驟而引古誼奪其至便而强其所
未習則毋乃苦難而不入乎善之入人也微猶
水之浸灌也漸其道莫若使人主常親事而益
務學事有所蔽而求通其心必虛學有所得而
===

欲聞及其方銳而開之以其所未悟使之優游
自趨饜飫自得悚然知正人之可恃而歡然見
其可親然後日有緝熙躬聽不倦正人益近用
事而主德日隆長久之計不勞而定矣故輔養
之術貴豫而轉移之機貴漸苟利宗社生靈而
已則毋欲速其功也哉

punctuated:
於世，一夫作難而七廟隳矣。夫周之所以久長者，其計得也；秦之所以亟絕者，其計失也。後之君臣，覩周之已事，鑒秦之覆轍，無亦兢兢於輔養之術哉？嗟乎！世道之趨，猶江河之不可返也。自堂陛森嚴，尊卑闊絕，人主之不能朝夕而臨羣臣也久矣。驟而引古誼，奪其至便而强其所未習，則毋乃苦難而不入乎？善之入人也微，猶水之浸灌也漸。其道莫若使人主常親事而益務學。事有所蔽而求通，其心必虛；學有所得而求益，其志必銳。夫能乘其至虛而牖之以其所欲聞，及其方銳而開之以其所未悟，使之優游自趨，饜飫自得，悚然知正人之可恃，而歡然見其可親，然後日有緝熙，躬聽不倦，正人益近用事，而主德日隆，長久之計不勞而定矣。故輔養之術貴豫，而轉移之機貴漸，苟利宗社生靈而已，則毋欲速其功也哉！

translation_en:
…the world; when a single man rose in rebellion, the seven ancestral temples were destroyed. That the Zhou endured so long was because its plan was sound; that the Qin was so quickly cut short was because its plan was flawed. Should not rulers and ministers of later ages, beholding the past deeds of the Zhou and taking warning from the overturned chariot of the Qin, be ever cautious and attentive to the art of assisting and nurturing the ruler? Alas! The trend of the world’s ways is like great rivers that cannot be turned back. Ever since the court steps grew stern and forbidding and the gulf between exalted and humble became vast, it has long been the case that the sovereign cannot appear before his assembled ministers morning and evening. If one abruptly cites ancient principles, depriving him of his greatest comforts and forcing upon him what he is unaccustomed to, will he not find it bitter and difficult, so that the counsel fails to enter his mind? Goodness enters a person subtly, just as water soaks and irrigates gradually. There is no better way than to have the sovereign constantly attend to affairs in person and increasingly devote himself to learning. When in affairs he encounters obscurities and seeks comprehension, his mind will necessarily be receptive; when in learning he gains understanding and seeks further progress, his will must be keen. If one can avail oneself of his utmost receptivity to enlighten him with what he wishes to hear, and seize upon his keenness of will to open up to him what he has not yet grasped—causing him to gravitate toward it at ease and find rich satisfaction of his own accord, until he realizes with awe that upright men can be relied upon and sees with joy that they are worthy of intimacy—then day by day there will be radiant progress, he will personally attend to governance without tiring, upright men will be drawn ever closer to hold authority, the ruler's virtue will daily flourish, and a plan for enduring stability will be established without toil. Therefore, in the art of assisting and nurturing the ruler, the essential thing is foresight, and in the pivotal work of transforming his disposition, the essential thing is gradualness. So long as it benefits the ancestral altars and the living people, let us not seek to rush its success!

Associate Examiner Director Lu comments: Words of response and praise in memorials of thanks mostly tend toward plagiarism and imitation. This piece is factual in its allusions and ornate in its diction, while an earnest sincerity of loyalty and devotion overflows between the lines. To have such a work in the examination compound is cause to congratulate the state on obtaining worthy talent.
Associate Examiner Chief Supervising Secretary Dai comments: Dignified and classic in rule, the finest of parallel prose (si-liu); it can serve as a model.
Associate Examiner Examining Editor Liu comments: Its cadence and rhetorical ornament are both exalted, and it does not lack elegance and rectitude. It truly has the style and bearing of the Tang writers; record it.
Associate Examiner Historiographer Wang comments: Classic, elegant, and finely paired, it captures the proper form for a memorial of gratitude, while loyal devotion warmly manifests itself in the words; it may serve as a model.
Associate Examiner Reader-in-Waiting Luo comments: Spreading forth ornate diction on the words of the inscriptions, it is solemn and classically elegant; it is fitting to record it as a model.
Examiner Academician Reader-in-Waiting Yu comments: Skilfully brings out the meaning of the bestowal of the inscriptions, and the phrasing is also precise and close-knit.
Examiner Grand Secretary Shen comments: Amidst its ornate beauty there is classic rule; record it.

translation_en:
… Imperial counsels, as earth and heaven harmonize in peace. The Emperor, ever mindful of timing and the subtlest beginnings, issues his admonitory charges; the minister, assisting day by day, receives and carries them forward. Favor brims over in these two compositions, and the honor surpasses that of the Three Bestowals. Your servant Sui, in utmost awe and trepidation, bows his head to the ground again and again.

I venture to reflect that when the sovereign and his chief ministers are entrusted with their charges, no way is more exalted than that of an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers; and when the constant teachings are free of fault, their purport is uniquely strict in admonition and caution. From the era of knotted cords onward, and ever since the Three Mounds and Eight Cords came into being, the Sovereign Xuan [the Yellow Emperor] was circumspect in speech, setting forth models upon his kerchiefs and armrests; the King of Xia sought remonstrance, engraving inscriptions upon his bell-frames and drum-stands; Tang’s basin urged daily renewal, a teaching preserved in the Golden Coffer (Jin gui); and King Wu’s window placed timely reverence first, drawing its source from the Cinnabar Book (Dan shu). In order that these might meet the eye and mind and thereby convey admonition, they borrowed visible forms to serve as models.

Yet once later, declining ages drifted away into Music Bureau songs, and the rulers of the times grew frivolous in the Airs of the States, the elegant proclamations and admonitory words ceased to echo between antiquity and the present. In tallying merits and boasting of martial achievements, ministers and rulers spoke with a single voice. Taking no thought for cautious diligence amid the myriad affairs of state, how could they manifest and bring forth pure, single-minded virtue? Even if carved with blossoms and woven with colors, how could the king’s words carry the weight of silken cords? Though engraved on tripods and incised in fine stone, how could the imperial measure be praised as gold and jade? Only a sage is able to create; does not this culture now reside right here?

This is because I humbly encounter Your Majesty [〇〇〇〇], who abundantly grasps the Mysterious Tally and gloriously presides over the Purple Pole. Yet foolish were those rebellious miscreants, who cunningly stirred up alarm along the frontiers! The King blazed with majestic wrath and charged the Seven Gathered Hosts to reverently execute heaven's punishment; the army marched forth with a righteous cause, and in a single battle the enemy was annihilated. The triumphant return took barely twenty-seven days, and the captives and spoils numbered sixteen thousand men. All of this came from receiving the guidance of Your grand strategy, and the victory was entirely the product of plans laid in the imperial ancestral temple—how could a mediocre and foolish servant like myself dare to usurp credit for the toil and merit? translation_en: … the beauty of Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou; and as wind and clouds tally in harmony, you look up to pursue the legacy of Yu and Xia. Repeatedly expounding in nearly a thousand words, your exhortations all converge upon a single purpose. Observing the patterns of heaven, all eight directions are illuminated; examining the ancient Way, the Six Classics remain immutable. Take the Golden Mirror (Jinjing) treatise of the Zhenguan era, which established teachings by drawing upon material things; or the Admonitions to the Bulwark of the State (Weicheng) of the Xianqing era, which borrowed from heaven to fix its title. Never before has there been a work that joins ruler and ministers upon silk scrolls, reveals sages and worthies within bamboo slips, and—when one unfolds the text to examine its substance—surpasses even the writings from Longdi, or—in absorbing antiquity and encompassing the present—goes far beyond the compositions of Huainan. Although in continuing and following the admirable wisdom of your ancestors, Your Majesty has indeed inherited their bright glory, yet when looking back to those meritorious worthies of old, your petty servant truly falls short of their very shadow and echo. How could I have expected that the exquisite calligraphy of dragons and phoenixes would be graciously bestowed upon one as lowly as a dog or horse? With finest jades arrayed before me, it is like borrowing wings to soar into the empyrean; with the jeweled astrolabe shining down upon me, it is like boring an aperture to behold a rainbow. Radiance bursts forth from the mushroom-seal case, and your praise is doubly more glorious than ceremonial robes of state. Your servant is ashamed of an understanding as narrow as spotting a leopard through a tube, and unworthy of the talent of a "neither-bear-nor-grisly" advisor. Roaming within the sage's realm where words fail, I gaze on tiptoe at your grand plans and think of spurring myself on; living beneath heaven and knowing only how to walk with bent back, I look up at the Great Image and grow ever more bewildered. Committing your words to memory is most earnest within my loyal heart, and by recounting and proclaiming them I wish to broadcast them in the bamboo annals of history. 文淵之馬革誓答
君恩伏願

translation_en:
… so that the jade-inscribed plaque shines together with the constellations Kui and Bi; and engraving it in stone to display in my hall, so that the precious bestowal endures as long as Heaven and Earth. How could it be said that Your servant is able to attribute beauty to his sovereign, idly boasting of the pieces in the Odes of Zhou? Truly it is the Emperor who thereupon composes songs, radiantly illuminating the chapters of the Documents of Yu. How dare I not send my sincere devotion racing to the imperial carriage, and join all my strength to the defense of the frontier screen? Ashamed that I lack the tiger's head of Marquis Dingyuan (Ban Chao 班超), I strive only to escape the censure of judicial officials; wrapped in a horsehide like Fubo (Ma Yuan 馬援, style Wenyuan 文淵), I swear to repay my Sovereign's grace.

I humbly pray that Your Sacred Virtue may steadily ascend, and Your Imperial Mind remain ever cautious: beholding the primal Creativity of Heaven in the celestial laws, and preserving abundant governance when the sun stands at its zenith; so that the imperial radiance shines forth and the myriad things are made bright, continuing the footsteps of the Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns in their swift course; and the Three Terrace stars gleam while the six auspicious signs respond, enlarging the grand design in which civil administration forms the warp and military power the woof. Your servant, overwhelmed beyond measure as he gazes up toward Heaven and looks upon the Sage with ardent emotion and grateful devotion, respectfully presents this memorial of thanks for the Emperor's hearing.

translation_en:
First Question

Comment by Associate Examiner Chief Supervising Secretary Qin: His Majesty honors and cares for the Sacred Mother; his pure filial piety not only equals that of Yu [Shun] and the Zhou kings, but far surpasses them. A scholar from the countryside is able to recount and praise each aspect one by one, and at the end of the essay speaks further of broadening filial piety. This especially shows the sincerity of his loyalty and affection; it should be selected for presentation to the Throne.

Comment by Associate Examiner Historiographer of the Second Class Yu: His Majesty in his pure filial piety honors and cares for the Sacred Mother, attaining the utmost in both ceremonial form and substance, far surpassing Yu and Zhou. You are able to extol these splendid virtues and further pursue their ultimate meaning by speaking of broadening filial piety. How you will one day transfer your filial piety into loyalty to the ruler can already be glimpsed here.

Comment by Associate Examiner Senior Compiler Sun: Coming as a scholar in straw sandals, he is nonetheless able to look up and perceive that the great filial piety of Our August Emperor does not stop merely at honoring and providing for his parent, and responds by citing the principles of broadening filial piety and pleasing one's parents. Your loyal sincerity overflows—it is not merely that the essay is skillful in praise. It should be selected.

Comment by Examiner Academician Reader-in-Waiting Yu: Our August Emperor's filial service to the Sacred Mother does not lie solely in honoring and caring for her. You are able to expound upon this and extend its implications; it is worthy of presentation to the Throne.

Comment by Examiner Grand Secretary Shen: The filial piety of emperors and kings differs from that of the common people. You are able to elaborate upon ancient principles, extol His Majesty's great filial piety, and set forth arguments on discoursing on the Way and nourishing the parental will, all stemming from earnest sincerity. One day we shall rely on your hand…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
立而化彰猶柄指而星靡故操一術而百
善至執一契而萬業明孝之謂也夫孝固
極彌綸叅贊之大而其旨則有切近精實
之歸乃其說自古記之矣孔子以始終言
孝謂事親事君立身而有曰當不義子不
可不爭曾子以小大言孝謂用力用勞不
匱而有曰君子諭父母於道孔曾而下代
有微言請摘其近醇而無疵者荀卿曰孝
者言爲可聞所以說遠行爲可見所以說
===
近其說在言行也董仲舒曰父之所生其
子長之所長養之所養成之不敢不致如
父之意其說在致意也劉向曰君子事親
以積德子者親之本也故親之所安子皆
供之其說在安親也揚雄曰孝莫大於寧
親寧親莫大於寧神寧神莫大於四表之
歡心其說在歡四表也是數者言人人殊
辭各有指而意實相成撮其要在立身推
其施在不匱要莫先於言行而積德施在

punctuated: 立而化彰，猶柄指而星靡。故操一術而百善至，執一契而萬業明，孝之謂也。夫孝固極彌綸叅贊之大，而其旨則有切近精實之歸，乃其說自古記之矣。孔子以始終言孝，謂事親、事君、立身，而有曰「當不義，子不可不爭」；曾子以小大言孝，謂用力、用勞、不匱，而有曰「君子諭父母於道」。孔、曾而下，代有微言，請摘其近醇而無疵者：荀卿曰：「孝者，言爲可聞，所以說遠；行爲可見，所以說近。」其說在言行也。董仲舒曰：「父之所生，其子長之；所長，養之；所養，成之。不敢不致如父之意。」其說在致意也。劉向曰：「君子事親以積德。子者，親之本也，故親之所安，子皆供之。」其說在安親也。揚雄曰：「孝莫大於寧親，寧親莫大於寧神，寧神莫大於四表之歡心。」其說在歡四表也。是數者，言人人殊，辭各有指，而意實相成。撮其要，在立身；推其施，在不匱。要莫先於言行，而積德施在
translation_en: … is established and moral transformation becomes manifest, just as the handle of the Dipper points and the stars follow. Therefore, to hold fast to a single art so that a hundred virtues arrive, and to grasp a single tally so that ten thousand enterprises become clear—this is what is meant by filial piety. Now, filial piety certainly reaches the utmost greatness of encompassing and assisting the cosmic order, yet its essential purport comes back to what is immediate, refined, and substantive; indeed, discourses on it have been recorded since antiquity. Confucius spoke of filial piety in terms of its beginning and end, referring to serving one's parents, serving one's ruler, and establishing oneself, while also saying, "When confronted with unrighteousness, a son cannot but remonstrate." Master Zeng (Zengzi) spoke of filial piety in terms of the small and the great, referring to exerting one's strength, expending one's toil, and unfailing provision, while also saying, "The gentleman leads his parents to the Way." From Confucius and Master Zeng onward, every age had its subtle words on the subject. Allow me to select those that are nearly pure and without flaw: Xun Qing (Xunzi) said, "For the filial, their words are fit to be heard, by which they please those afar; their conduct is fit to be seen, by which they please those nearby." His teaching lies in words and conduct. Dong Zhongshu said, "What the father gives birth to, his son brings to growth; what the father brings to growth, he nourishes; what the father nourishes, he brings to completion, never daring not to fulfill the father's wishes." His teaching lies in fulfilling one's father's wishes. Liu Xiang said, "The gentleman serves his parents by accumulating virtue. The son is the root of the parents' joy; therefore, whatever brings peace to the parents, the son provides it all." His teaching lies in bringing peace to one's parents. Yang Xiong said, "In filial piety, nothing is greater than bringing peace to one's parents; in bringing peace to one's parents, nothing is greater than bringing peace to their spirits; in bringing peace to their spirits, nothing is greater than winning the joyful hearts of the four reaches of the world." His teaching lies in winning the joy of the four reaches. Among these several thinkers, the words vary from person to person and each phrasing has its own specific aim, yet their meanings actually complement one another. To sum up their essentials, it lies in establishing oneself; to extend their application, it lies in unfailing provision. In essentials, nothing comes before words and conduct, while accumulating virtue and extending application lie in…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
深宮燕閒亦式亦入乎
大廷建白惟時惟幾乎則朝而聽政晝而訪
問夕而修令儲精垂思緝熈帝圖斯懿善
不違乎身可以廣身養之孝矣
皇上慎乃儉德減織造矣却獻馬矣然
尚方供奉意少約乎歲時錫予意稍裁乎則
弗作無益弗貴異物弗重難得戒非僻絕
尤麗以膺
壽禔福斯耳目不違乎心可以廣心養之孝矣
===
言出而遵若四時事舉而欽於昊命
聖母志無不得矣然
宮府有體可修舉乎治敎有則可彰明乎從
道乃衷則安從理乃義則榮從度乃敬則
修飾審於從不從之間而致畏信端愨以
慎行之斯思慮不違乎親可以廣親養之
孝矣而猶進焉乾坤父母民物胞與咸寄
皇上之一身則晝選男德以象穀明夜靜女德
以杜私謁所以悅邦家也薪槱賢才以登

translation_en:
… Even in the leisure of the deep palace, do You take models and absorb admonition? When memorials and proposals are presented in the grand court, are You ever timely and mindful of subtle incipiencies? Thus, holding court to hear governance in the morning, making inquiries during the day, and revising ordinances in the evening—storing up vital energy, applying deep thought, and continuing to make bright the imperial plan—in this way, admirable goodness will never depart from Your person, and You may broaden the filial piety of nourishing with Your person.

Your Majesty is careful of the virtue of frugality: You have reduced the imperial textile manufacturing and rejected the presentation of tribute horses. Yet in the supplies furnished by the Directorate for Imperial Manufactories, might Your intention be to economize a little further? In the seasonal bestowal of gifts, might Your intention be to curtail them slightly? Then by not making useless things, not prizing strange objects, and not valuing hard-to-get goods, by guarding against what is improper and perverse and cutting off extraordinary finery so as to receive longevity and enjoy blessings—in this way, the ears and eyes will not go against the mind, and You may broaden the filial piety of nourishing with the mind.

When her words go forth, You comply with them like the four seasons; when affairs are undertaken, You revere them like the mandate of vast Heaven; thus there is nothing in which the wishes of the Sacred Mother are not fulfilled. Yet the inner palace and outer court have their proper system—can it be repaired and upheld? Governance and instruction have their standards—can they be made illustrious and clear? Following the Way out of inner sincerity brings peace; following principle out of righteousness brings glory; following regulation out of reverence brings refinement. By discriminating carefully between when to follow and when not to follow, and bringing forth awe, trustworthiness, uprightness, and謹sincerity to practice them cautiously—in this way, Your thoughts and deliberations will not go against Your parent, and You may broaden the filial piety of nourishing Your parent.

And going still further: Heaven and Earth are the father and mother, and the people and myriad things are brothers and companions, all entrusted to the single person of Your Majesty. Thus, by day selecting masculine virtue to emulate the bright nourishment of the sun, and by night quieting feminine virtue to block private audiences—this is the means to bring joy to the state and the royal house; gathering worthy talents like firewood to advance…

同考試官編修劉　批〔正學湮而當世游談士窮割釋氏竄儒指其中言紕楚莫能辨詰也即執斯策以諳觀道本一一數其非而闢之庶幾臻鄒孟敛焉〕
punctuated:
治理，浸惠萌庶以致雍熈，所以悅臣民也；崇功報德以章祖禰，憲時居利以則天地，所以悅神明也。夫如是，則一孝立而百順聚，百順聚而萬化洽，德足以媲重華，年可以過周曆，彼庚桑楚所稱「至誠之至，有感必應」者在是矣。夫文實配行，禮養俱施，此因於聖心，祕於宮闈，非疎逖所聞也。將順王猷，宣揚國美，使聖孝以光，聖化以烈，執事責也，愚生又敢知焉。

第二問
同考試官編修劉批：正學湮而當世游談士剽剟釋氏，窟儒指其中，言糺棼莫能辨詰也。即執斯策以證，觀道本，一一數其非而闢之，庶幾臻廓如之效焉。
translation_en:
… [employing worthy talents to advance] governance, and steeping the common people in favor so as to bring about harmonious prosperity—this is the means to delight subjects and the people; exalting功 (merit) and repaying virtue so as to make illustrious the imperial ancestors, and modeling on the seasons and dwelling in what is beneficial so as to pattern oneself after Heaven and Earth—this is the means to delight the spirits and gods. If it be thus, then once filial piety is established, all things in compliance gather together; once all things in compliance gather together, the myriad transformations pervade everywhere. His virtue will suffice to match that of Chonghua [Shun], and his years of reign may surpass the calendar of Zhou. What Gengsang Chu 庚桑楚 spoke of as "the utmost of supreme sincerity, wherein every stimulus necessarily meets with a response," lies right here! Now, matching outward form with实质 (substance) in practice, and bestowing both ritual propriety and filial nurture—these stem from the Sacred Heart and are kept secret within the palace chambers; they are not things that one who is distant and humble gets to hear of. To comply with and further the Kingly plan, and to proclaim and spread abroad the beauties of the state, causing the Sacred Filial Piety to shine forth and the Sacred Transformation to be glorious—that is the responsibility of Your Excellencies the Examiners; how would this foolish student dare presume to know of it?

Second Question
Comment (pi) by Associate Examiner Compiler (Bianxiu) Liu 劉: Since orthodox learning became obscured, the wandering talkers of the present age have plagiarized and pilfered from the Buddhists, making their nest within Confucianism and pointing to its core as their own; their words are so tangled and confused that no one is able to distinguish and challenge them. If one takes up this policy essay as verification, observes the fundamental source of the Way, and enumerates their errors one by one to refute them, one may perhaps achieve the effect of sweeping the realm clear.

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
同考試官編修盛批釋氏得溷吾道與學者易祟釋
氏本於似是之辨未明耳是作剖析毫釐末復歸之反經人心自此
有真是矣
考試官侍讀學士秦批儒釋易溷間不容髮是能縷析其旨
剨切其微彼為釋說者不攻而破矣
考試官大學士申批世儒竊似亂真害道最甚是作反復
辨詰辭嚴義正有關世道者錄之
聖人之道詎不較然貞夫一哉而胡後世
學者之岐之也蓋有昧道而背者有似道
===
而非者二者皆足以損吾道也而似是之
害無大焉何者彼以背之之說撓之此以
似之之說亂之也背之說可以棓吾道之
粗而似之說乃以蝕吾道之精背之說可
以淆庸衆之心而似之說乃以瞽賢知之
見背之說則訾纇而易辨而似之說善逃
遁而無倪蓋其始也厭聖道為尋常借異
說為門户其既也叛吾道入其中其究也
又驅吾道佐之而與吾道角立為教甚使

聖人之道，詎不較然貞夫一哉？而胡後世學者之岐之也？蓋有昧道而背者，有似道而非者，二者皆足以損吾道也，而似是之害無大焉。何者？彼以背之之說撓之，此以似之之說亂之也。背之說，可以棓吾道之粗；而似之說，乃以蝕吾道之精。背之說，可以淆庸衆之心；而似之說，乃以瞽賢知之見。背之說，則訾纇而易辨；而似之說，善逃遁而無倪。蓋其始也，厭聖道為尋常，借異說為門户；其既也，叛吾道入其中；其究也，又驅吾道佐之，而與吾道角立為教，甚使…
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Compiler Sheng comments: That the Buddhists have been able to muddle our Way, and that scholars are easily bewitched by Buddhism, stems simply from the distinction between what merely resembles the truth and the truth itself not having been made clear. This essay dissects the matter down to the finest hair's breadth, and at the end returns to the principle of restoring the constant norm; from this, human minds will possess the true right.

Examiner Academician Reader-in-Waiting Qin comments: Confucianism and Buddhism are easily confounded, with scarcely a hair's breadth between them. This essay is able to analyze their purport thread by thread and incisively lay bare their subtleties; those who advocate Buddhist doctrines are thus refuted without even being attacked.

Examiner Grand Secretary Shen comments: Contemporary Confucians steal what merely resembles the truth to confound the genuine, doing the greatest harm to the Way. This essay repeatedly debates and cross-examines the issue; its language is stern and its principles upright. Because it is of consequence to the moral order of the world, I record it.

Is the Way of the Sages not manifestly constant and unified in the One? Why, then, have scholars of later ages caused it to diverge? It is because there are those who, blind to the Way, turn their backs upon it, and there are those who resemble the Way and yet are not of it. Both are sufficient to impair our Way, yet no harm is greater than that of what merely resembles the truth. Why is this? The former obstructs it with doctrines that openly oppose it, whereas the latter confounds it with doctrines that closely resemble it. Doctrines that oppose it can strike at the coarse externals of our Way, whereas doctrines that resemble it erode the very essence of our Way. Doctrines that oppose it can confuse the minds of the ordinary multitude, whereas doctrines that resemble it blind the perception of the worthy and the wise. Doctrines that oppose it are flawed and easy to distinguish, whereas doctrines that resemble it are skilled at evasion and leave no trace to grasp. In the beginning, such men disdain the Way of the Sages as commonplace and borrow heterodox doctrines to establish their own sects; thereafter, they betray our Way and enter into those doctrines; and in the end, they even press our Way into service to assist them, standing in rivalry with our Way as a competing teaching, going so far as to cause…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
吾道晦而幾絕噫其禍難言哉執事憂之
而慨古昔所稱學術者為說是不足辯也
雖然問及之矣詎敢遺乎愚嘗謂道原出
於天大明於孔氏孔氏以前有操行而無
論議孔氏以來有論議而絕蹊徑孔氏以
後有蹊徑而鮮奇僻秦漢以來有奇僻而
短剽攘譬之絲出於繭而愈引愈棼水決
於涯而浸流浸遠有不可以端緒索而隄
防止者是故莊周述九家焉自詩書禮樂
===
===
而外有老聃關尹禽墨者流遵俶詭洸洋
以與吾人為難矯世齊物各得一察以自
好而其於道也恣荀卿非十二家焉自子
思孟軻而下有它囂魏牟陳史者流指聖
人為僻遠幽隱眩名實欹正不自知其喬
宇嵬瑣而其於道也舛馬遷論六家指要
班固載九家於藝文志雜儒道於方伎竝
稱而詆議之曰寡要少功雖其操術輔理
百家不易而其於道也離是數者各因其

punctuated: 吾道晦而幾絕。噫！其禍難言哉！執事憂之，而慨古昔所稱學術者為說，是不足辯也。雖然，問及之矣，詎敢遺乎？愚嘗謂：道原出於天，大明於孔氏。孔氏以前，有操行而無論議；孔氏以來，有論議而絕蹊徑；孔氏以後，有蹊徑而鮮奇僻；秦漢以來，有奇僻而短剽攘。譬之絲出於繭，而愈引愈棼；水決於涯，而浸流浸遠，有不可以端緒索而隄防止者。是故莊周述九家焉，自《詩》、《書》、《禮》、《樂》而外，有老聃、關尹、禽墨者流，遵俶詭洸洋，以與吾人為難，矯世齊物，各得一察以自好，而其於道也恣。荀卿非十二家焉，自子思、孟軻而下，有它囂、魏牟、陳史者流，指聖人為僻遠幽隱，眩名實，欹正，不自知其喬宇嵬瑣，而其於道也舛。馬遷論六家指要，班固載九家於《藝文志》，雜儒道於方伎竝稱，而詆議之曰：「寡要少功。」雖其操術輔理，百家不易，而其於道也離。是數者，各因其
translation_en:
… our Way was obscured and nearly extinguished. Alas, its disaster is hard to put into words! Your Excellency worries about this and laments the doctrines of what were called scholarly arts in antiquity; these are indeed not worth refuting. Even so, since your question touches upon them, how could I dare omit them?

I have previously maintained that the origin of the Way comes from Heaven and was greatly illuminated by Confucius (Kongshi 孔氏). Before Confucius, there was moral conduct without theoretical discourse; from Confucius onward, there was discourse without devious bypaths; after Confucius, there were bypaths but rarely anything bizarre or perverse; and since the Qin and Han dynasties, there has been the bizarre and perverse, yet lacking outright plagiarism and usurpation. It is like silk drawn from a cocoon that becomes more tangled the more it is pulled, or water breaching a bank that flows ever further as it spreads—something that cannot be traced by its loose ends or held back by dikes.

Therefore, Zhuang Zhou (莊周) recounted the Nine Schools: outside of the Odes (Shi 詩), Documents (Shu 書), Rites (Li 禮), and Music (Yue 樂), there were the likes of Lao Dan (老聃), Guan Yin (關尹), Qin Guli (禽滑釐), and Mo Di (墨翟), who pursued the bizarre, paradoxical, and boundless to challenge us; seeking to rectify the world or equalize all things, each grasped a single partial insight with which to please himself, and in relation to the Way they were unrestrained. Xun Qing (荀卿, Xunzi) criticized the Twelve Masters: from Zisi (子思) and Meng Ke (孟軻, Mencius) downward, there were the likes of Tuo Xiao (它囂), Wei Mou (魏牟), Chen Zhong (陳仲), and Shi Qiu (史鰌), who pointed to the sages as out-of-the-way and obscure, confused names and realities, tilted what was upright, and did not realize their own pretentiousness and pettiness; in relation to the Way they were perverse. Sima Qian (馬遷) discussed the essential points of the Six Schools, and Ban Gu (班固) recorded the Nine Schools in his "Treatise on Literature" (Yiwen zhi 藝文志), lumping the Confucian Way together with technical arts and criticizing it by saying that it "has few essentials and achieves little result." Although in practicing their arts to assist governance the Hundred Schools could not replace them, in relation to the Way they diverged from it. These several groups each based…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
所見以爲言各即其言以爲道然不能爲
道病也蓋聖人之道若日中天陰陽者知
爲陰陽墨者知爲墨道德者知爲道德名
法者知爲名法農雜者知爲農雜畛分畛
列較然蒼素方是時諸子百家尚折衷於
吾道以爲準至唐宋而後釋老二家者出
竄入於吾道而尤不敢溷至於宋季而釋
氏與吾道幾溷而一之然猶陰附陽闢未
敢顯然推吾儒而爲之役也乃今有大謬
===
不然者矣愚請得更僕數之今之學者本
無定是也而曰當體便是動用即乖見謂
吾儒無私順感之體而不知此即釋氏不
思善惡者也夫中無定體惟道是體安得
妄執之而一無所用本有顯慝也而曰有
過即使人知不煩掩覆見謂吾儒好惡不
欺之誠而不知此即釋氏不礙事障者也
夫過而不改是爲過矣又安得怙終而不
悛不顧大閑無事繩檢所存出於爲利也

punctuated: 所見以爲言，各即其言以爲道，然不能爲道病也。蓋聖人之道，若日中天，陰陽者知爲陰陽，墨者知爲墨，道德者知爲道德，名法者知爲名法，農雜者知爲農雜，畛分畛列，較然蒼素。方是時，諸子百家尚折衷於吾道以爲準。至唐、宋而後，釋、老二家者出，竄入於吾道，而尤不敢溷。至於宋季，而釋氏與吾道幾溷而一之，然猶陰附陽闢，未敢顯然推吾儒而爲之役也。乃今有大謬不然者矣，愚請得更僕數之。今之學者，本無定是也，而曰「當體便是，動用即乖」，見謂吾儒無私順感之體，而不知此即釋氏「不思善惡」者也。夫中無定體，惟道是體，安得妄執之而一無所用？本有顯慝也，而曰「有過即使人知，不煩掩覆」，見謂吾儒好惡不欺之誠，而不知此即釋氏「不礙事障」者也。夫過而不改，是爲過矣，又安得怙終而不悛？不顧大閑，無事繩檢，所存出於爲利也，
translation_en: … what they personally perceived to formulate their doctrines, and each took their own doctrines to be the Way; yet they could not do real harm to the Way. For the Way of the Sages was like the sun at mid-heaven: followers of the Yin-Yang school were recognized as Yin-Yang; Mohists were recognized as Mohists; followers of the Way and Its Virtue (Daoists) were recognized as followers of the Way and Its Virtue; Logicians and Legalists were recognized as Logicians and Legalists; Agriculturalists and Eclectics were recognized as Agriculturalists and Eclectics. Their boundaries were distinctly drawn and arrayed, as clearly distinguishable as black and white. At that time, the Various Masters and Hundred Schools still took our Way as the standard by which to weigh their judgments. From the Tang and Song dynasties onward, the two schools of Buddhism and Daoism emerged and infiltrated our Way, yet even then they did not dare to confound themselves with it. By the end of the Song, Buddhism and our Way were nearly confounded into one; even so, people secretly adhered to it while openly refuting it, not yet daring to blatantly push our Confucianism into its service. Nowadays, however, there is something grossly contrary to this! Allow me to enumerate these points at length, even if it takes reliefs of attendants. Scholars of today have no fixed principle of right to begin with, yet they say, "The immediate substance is right in itself; the moment it is stirred into function, it goes awry." They suppose this to be our Confucian substance of selflessness and responsive compliance, not realizing that this is actually the Buddhists' "thinking of neither good nor evil." Now, equilibrium has no fixed substance—only the Way is its substance; how can one rashly cling to it and make no functional use of it whatsoever? They have glaring vices to begin with, yet they say, "When one has a fault, simply let others know of it without bothering to cover it up." They suppose this to be our Confucian sincerity of having no self-deception in one's likes and dislikes, not realizing that this is actually the Buddhists' "being unhindered by phenomenal obstacles." Now, to have a fault and not reform is indeed a fault; how can one persist in it to the end without repenting? Disregarding the great moral bounds and dispensing with self-restraint, what they harbor in their hearts stems from the pursuit of profit, …

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
而曰無點于躬倂釋氏出世間法而竊之
於吾儒慎修之道謂何不惜頂踵以急天
下所存出於為名高也而曰大公無我卽
托釋氏所謂利他行者乃吾儒推恩之術
當不若是道不可以凌躐進也彼持速之
說者曰頓悟在心無法可得舉積累之功
而皆厭棄焉此釋氏一念證佛之說為誕
而已矣道不可以多岐為也彼持紛之說
者曰心逐事生不可除盡舉天下事無纖
鉅而柴其中焉此釋氏萬法惟心之說為
溺而已矣玩忽世故吐棄物理塊然自便
附釋氏寂空之說而曰吾主靜也此非世
之人枯槁赴淵者之所好與吾儒動靜交
養者大有徑廷焉悖而已矣己私未淨而
謬曰天地萬物俱在掌中此夫病目而空
生華者也己行未修而妄曰聖賢地位不
出足下此夫標指而幻見月者也知未通
也而欲攝宇宙於毫端是身適越而望冥

鉅而柴其中焉此釋氏萬法惟心之說爲
溺而已矣玩忽世故吐棄物理塊然自便
附釋氏寂空之說而曰吾主靜也此非世
之人枯槁赴淵者之所好與吾儒動靜交
養者大有徑廷焉悖而已矣已私未淨而
謬曰天地萬物俱在掌中此夫病目而空
生華者也已行未修而妄曰聖賢地位不
出足下此夫標指而幻見月者也知未通
也而欲攝宇宙於毫端是身適越而望冥
punctuated: 而曰「無點于躬」，倂釋氏出世間法而竊之，於吾儒慎修之道謂何？不惜頂踵以急天下，所存出於為名高也，而曰「大公無我」，卽托釋氏所謂利他行者，乃吾儒推恩之術當不若是。道不可以凌躐進也，彼持速之說者曰：「頓悟在心，無法可得。」舉積累之功而皆厭棄焉，此釋氏一念證佛之說，為誕而已矣。道不可以多岐為也，彼持紛之說者曰：「心逐事生，不可除盡。」舉天下事無纖鉅而柴其中焉，此釋氏萬法惟心之說，為溺而已矣。玩忽世故，吐棄物理，塊然自便，附釋氏寂空之說，而曰「吾主靜也」，此非世之人枯槁赴淵者之所好與？吾儒動靜交養者大有徑廷焉，悖而已矣。己私未淨，而謬曰「天地萬物俱在掌中」，此夫病目而空生華者也；己行未修，而妄曰「聖賢地位不出足下」，此夫標指而幻見月者也。知未通也，而欲攝宇宙於毫端，是身適越而望冥
translation_en: …yet they say, "Nothing stains my person," stealing even the Buddhists' dharma of transcending the world; what does this say of our Confucian Way of careful self-cultivation? They do not spare themselves from head to heel in rushing to the aid of the world, though what they harbor in their hearts comes from seeking lofty fame; yet they say, "This is supreme impartiality and selflessness," borrowing what the Buddhists call the practice of benefiting others—whereas our Confucian art of extending kindness should not be like this. The Way cannot be advanced by skipping steps; yet those who uphold the doctrine of rapidity say, "Sudden enlightenment lies in the mind; there is no dharma to be attained," and they spurn and discard all the work of gradual accumulation. This is the Buddhist doctrine of realizing Buddhahood in a single thought, which is nothing more than absurdity. The Way cannot be practiced through branching paths; yet those who uphold the doctrine of multiplicity say, "The mind arises in pursuit of affairs and cannot be completely cleared away," and they take all the affairs of the world, whether minute or great, and clutter their inner minds with them. This is the Buddhist doctrine that the myriad dharmas are mind-only, which is nothing more than infatuation. Trifling with worldly affairs and casting aside the principles of things, they sit like clods at their own ease, attaching themselves to the Buddhist doctrine of quiescence and emptiness while saying, "I make stillness my master." Is this not what is favored by those in the world who wither away and cast themselves into the abyss? It differs vastly from our Confucian mutual nourishment of activity and stillness, and is nothing more than perversity. Their own selfish desires are not yet purified, yet they absurdly say, "Heaven, earth, and the myriad things are all within the palm of my hand"—this is like one with diseased eyes seeing flowers appear in empty space. Their own conduct is not yet cultivated, yet they recklessly say, "The station of sages and worthies goes no further than beneath my feet"—this is like one pointing a finger and illusorily seeing the moon. Their knowledge is not yet penetrating, yet they wish to gather the cosmos onto the tip of a hair; this is like setting out in person for Yue while gazing toward Mount Ming…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
山者也學未充也而遽委文字於理障是
枵腹而哆爲果然者也夫若是者其曷以
故哉始焉擇術不精旣焉執德不固起於
毫釐之差卒於千里之謬彼釋氏竊聖人
之緒餘世儒復盜釋氏之土苴聖人曰心
性釋氏亦曰心性聖人曰知覺釋氏亦曰
圓覺聖人曰靜虛釋氏亦曰靜定釋氏以
緣識爲性情而欲斷之世儒以義理爲情
性而亦欲斷之釋氏以君臣父子爲假合
===
而欲離之世儒以綱常倫理爲見境而亦
欲離之釋氏以山河大地爲幻妄而欲空
之世儒以中和位育爲能事而亦欲空之
微獨聖人之學彼所懵然卽釋氏之旨亦
未能闖其藩籬究厥奧窔不過設浮游之
辭以聳攝其黨與令天下嚄嚄然交臂而
拜同聲而贊彼逌然自謂聖人而徒視天
下矣而豈知其爲世道蠹也不甚熾哉愚
請得名其蠹偶覩一班輒居全覺獨取隻

translation_en: …Mountains; and before one's learning is full, to hastily dismiss written words as obstacles to principle is to have an empty belly while bragging that one is stuffed full. Now, why are they like this? At first, they are not discerning in choosing their art; subsequently, they are not steadfast in holding to virtue. It begins with the discrepancy of a hair's breadth and ends in an error of a thousand miles. Those Buddhists stole the leftover remnants of the Sages, and contemporary Confucians in turn pilfer the dregs and chaff of the Buddhists. The Sages speak of mind and nature, and the Buddhists also speak of mind and nature; the Sages speak of perception and awareness, and the Buddhists also speak of perfect enlightenment; the Sages speak of quiescence and emptiness, and the Buddhists also speak of quiescence and meditative concentration. The Buddhists regard conditioned consciousness as one's nature and feelings and wish to sever it, while contemporary Confucians regard moral principle as feelings and nature and likewise wish to sever it. The Buddhists regard ruler and minister, father and son as provisional combinations and wish to depart from them, while contemporary Confucians regard the Three Bonds, the Five Constant Virtues, and human moral relations as mere phenomenal realms and likewise wish to depart from them. The Buddhists regard mountains, rivers, and the great earth as illusory and false and wish to empty them out, while contemporary Confucians regard equilibrium and harmony, and establishing order and nourishing all things, as mere technical feats and likewise wish to empty them out. Not only are they utterly ignorant of the learning of the Sages, even as to the purport of the Buddhists, they have failed to peer past their outer fence or probe their innermost recesses. They do no more than contrive floating, ungrounded words to excite and awe their partisans, making the whole world clamorously join arms to bow before them and praise them with one voice. Complacently, they call themselves sages and look down upon the world as nothing—yet how could they know that as wood-borers eating away at the Way of the world, they are raging all too fiercely? title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
字自標法門其名為譎韆鞦仁義纓璅道
德駕言墮黜自决含珠其名為狂身擁臯
比口傳木鐸片言契合許以證聖其名為
僭見巧若狙赴機如鶻乘人闚捷不避阮
穽其名為賊與之語大人則傾蓋劇譚目
為上乘與之語細人則跏趺終日棄為鈍
根人誠賢矣不入其黨則指之曰未聞道
也奚而賢誠不肖矣一及其門則芘之曰
是知嚮道者也不保其往或稍抑必借巧
===
以更揚或此負則要彼而求勝至使賢知
者聞之駭然喪其所守而不肖者貿貿若
大夢而莫之醒且舉天下姦慝莫不逋藪
其中此五帝所必放三王所必殛也豈明
盛之世所宜有哉特以其彌近似而大亂
真故欲名為異端而實則非異將目為外
道而其道非外譬之疾然是中內關者也
外關之疾攻而藥之可旦夕愈內關之疾
結轖於肺腑附着於膏肓鍼砭之所不加

translation_en: … word and proclaiming it as one's own Dharma-gate: the name for this is deceit. Treating benevolence and righteousness as a mere swing-set and morality as a trifling shackle, fabricating talk of casting off bodily form and intelligence, and digging into oneself as though splitting open jaws to seize a pearl: the name for this is madness. Wrapping oneself in the lecturer's tiger skin and claiming one's mouth transmits the wooden clapper-bell of heaven, then upon a single matching phrase granting someone certification of sagehood: the name for this is usurpation. Eyeing clever tricks like a monkey, pouncing on opportunities like a falcon, taking advantage of others and spying out shortcuts without shrinking from pitfalls and traps [?]: the name for this is villainy. When one speaks with them of great men, they lower their carriage canopies to converse intensely, regarding them as the Supreme Vehicle; when one speaks with them of humble folk, they sit cross-legged all day and cast them aside as having dull faculties. Though a man be truly worthy, if he does not join their faction, they point at him and say, "He has not heard the Way—how can he be worthy?" Though a man be truly unworthy, once he reaches their gate, they shelter him and say, "This is one who knows to turn toward the Way; we do not hold his past against him." If they are slightly curbed, they inevitably borrow cleverness to exalt themselves all the more; if they suffer defeat on one point, they ambush the other side elsewhere to seek victory. It comes to the point that when the worthy and wise hear them, they are startled into losing what they hold fast to, while the unworthy stumble about blindly as if in a great dream from which none can wake them. Moreover, all the wicked and villainous people in the world flee into their midst as a refuge. Such men are those whom the Five Emperors would surely have banished and the Three Kings would surely have executed—how could it be right for them to exist in an enlightened and flourishing age! Yet precisely because they seem ever closer to the truth while throwing the genuine into great confusion, if one wishes to name them heretical doctrines, in reality they do not appear alien; if one is about to regard them as outside teachings, their Way is not from the outside. To compare it to an illness, this is one that strikes the internal vital passages. title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
湯液之所不能灑而及也然則如之何其
一之孟子曰反經而已矣經者聖人之道
而執事之所謂大中至正者也
明天子在上躬行率先一道德而同風俗游談
有禁剙學聚徒有禁其設敎也本六經而
斥百氏其尚賢也先實行而後虛聲其論
才也貴適用而賤竅語將見聖人之經旣
正則邪說之害自息矣詩曰雨雪漉漉見
晛曰消則今日之謂哉
===

湯液之所不能灑而及也。然則如之何其一之？孟子曰：「反經而已矣。」經者，聖人之道，而執事之所謂大中至正者也。明天子在上，躬行率先，一道德而同風俗，游談有禁，剙學聚徒有禁。其設敎也，本六經而斥百氏；其尚賢也，先實行而後虛聲；其論才也，貴適用而賤竅語。將見聖人之經旣正，則邪說之害自息矣。《詩》曰：「雨雪漉漉，見晛曰消。」則今日之謂哉！

translation_en:
…nor can decoctions wash them away or reach them. How then are we to unify them? Mencius said: "Simply return to the constant standard." The constant standard is the Way of the Sages, which Your Excellency has called the supremely central and utterly correct. With our enlightened Son of Heaven above, leading the way through personal practice to unify morality and harmonize customs, idle disputation is prohibited, and founding novel doctrines to gather disciples is prohibited. In establishing instruction, he grounds it in the Six Classics and rejects the Hundred Schools; in exalting the worthy, he puts actual conduct first and empty reputation last; in evaluating talent, he prizes practical utility and disdains hollow talk [? 竅語]. We shall soon see that once the constant standard of the Sages is rectified, the harm of perverse doctrines will cease of its own accord. The Classic of Odes (Shijing) says: "The sleet and snow fall thick and fast, / But when they see the sun's heat, they melt away." Is this not spoken of our own day?

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
國家長治久安超軼往代其本在國勢重而人心安子能紬繹言之誠爲達識宜錄
同考試官侍讀羅批國勢人心兩者我
朝超軼前代遠甚子能鋪陳其盛而末歸之正紀綱厚德澤是足賛
廟謨矣錄之
考試官侍讀學士秦批論古事甚核而策今務悉中機宜儻
所謂經國士非耶
考試官大學士申批援古證今洞晰理亂之繇而持論正
大是通達國體者
天下之事有大可患而卒不能爲患者非
===
恃其有濟變之權而恃國有不可拔之勢
非恃其有扶危之術而恃人有不忍叛之
心夫國勢不可使靡也要於常重已耳人
心不可使離也要於常安已耳國勢重則
赫聲濯靈形體以強而天下罔敢越軼人
心安則含膏飲澤氣脈以鬯而天下罔敢
背攜卽有猝至之變不可測之虞上下怵
愕方深以爲患而竟帖然無事者其本固
也不然勢靡則易傾心離則易玩一旦緩

考試官侍讀學秦　批　〔論古事甚核而策今務悉中機宜儻〕
所謂經國之非耶
考試官大學士申　批　〔援古證今洞晰理亂之繇而持論正〕
大足通達國體者
天下之事有大可患而卒不能爲患者非
===
恃其有濟變之權而恃國有不可拔之勢
非恃其有扶危之術而恃人有不忍叛之
心夫國勢不可使靡也要於常重已耳人
心不可使離也要於常安已耳國勢重則
赫聲濯靈形體以强而天下罔敢越軼人
心安則合膏飲澤氣脈以啗而天下罔敢
背攜即有猝至之變不可測之虞上下怵
愕方深以爲患而竟帖然無事者其本固
也不然勢靡則易傾心離則易玩一旦緩
punctuated:
國家長治久安，超軼往代，其本在國勢重而人心安。子能紬繹言之，誠爲達識，宜錄。
同考試官侍讀羅批：國勢、人心兩者，我朝超軼前代遠甚。子能鋪陳其盛，而末歸之正紀綱、厚德澤，是足賛廟謨矣，錄之。
考試官侍讀學士秦批：論古事甚核，而策今務悉中機宜，儻所謂經國士非耶？
考試官大學士申批：援古證今，洞晰理亂之繇，而持論正大，是通達國體者。
天下之事，有大可患而卒不能爲患者，非恃其有濟變之權，而恃國有不可拔之勢；非恃其有扶危之術，而恃人有不忍叛之心。夫國勢不可使靡也，要於常重已耳；人心不可使離也，要於常安已耳。國勢重，則赫聲濯靈，形體以強，而天下罔敢越軼；人心安，則含膏飲澤，氣脈以鬯，而天下罔敢背攜。卽有猝至之變、不可測之虞，上下怵愕，方深以爲患，而竟帖然無事者，其本固也。不然，勢靡則易傾，心離則易玩，一旦緩
translation_en:
… dynasty's enduring peace and stability surpass those of past eras, fundamentally because the state's momentum is weighty and the people's hearts are settled. That you are able to draw out and expound upon this truly shows far-reaching insight; it ought to be selected for inclusion.
Associate Examiner Reader-in-waiting Luo comments: In both the momentum of the state and the hearts of the people, our dynasty surpasses previous eras by far. You are able to set forth this flourishing state in detail, and at the end trace it back to rectifying the state's discipline and deepening benevolent grace; this is sufficient to assist the deliberations of the imperial ancestral temple. Select it for inclusion.
Examiner Reader-in-waiting Academician Qin comments: The discussion of ancient affairs is very well-verified, and the policy proposals for current affairs all hit the mark of what is opportune. Is this not what is called a scholar capable of ordering the state?
Examiner Grand Secretary Shen comments: Citing antiquity to substantiate the present, it thoroughly discerns the causes of order and disorder, while maintaining an upright and grand argument; this is someone who thoroughly understands the fundamental structure of the state.

In the affairs of the world, that there are things giving great cause for alarm which ultimately fail to become disasters is not because one relies on having the权 [expedient power] to remedy crises, but because one relies on the state having an unshakable momentum; not because one relies on having techniques to prop up peril, but because one relies on the people having hearts that cannot bear to rebel. Now, the momentum of the state must not be allowed to weaken; the essential point lies simply in keeping it constantly weighty. The hearts of the people must not be allowed to become alienated; the essential point lies simply in keeping them constantly settled. When the momentum of the state is weighty, its majestic renown and radiant authority strengthen the body politic, and none in the world dare to overstep or transgress. When the hearts of the people are settled, they savour enriching moisture and drink in benevolent grace, the vital arteries flow smoothly, and none in the world dare to turn their backs or stray. Even if there are sudden upheavals or unforeseeable perils, such that superiors and inferiors are struck with alarm and deeply regard them as disasters, yet in the end everything remains calm and without incident, it is because the foundation is secure. Otherwise, if momentum weakens, it is easy to topple; if hearts are alienated, it is easy to breed contempt. Once an emergency…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
奚將焉恃乎蓋自漢而下凡爲天下大患
者五孝景時吳楚七國連兵內嚮天子爲
屈意誅謀臣謝過空國都而拒戰僅乃勝
之何岌岌也其患在諸侯王强大而不軌
魏晉以來羌胡鮮卑降者率居塞內諸郡
劉淵一倡而幷雍之胡響臻神州遂陸沉
矣其患在華夷雜處而疎於防唐自太和
以後士卒殺主帥邀節鉞若盧龍陝虢宣
武諸軍比比而是朝廷莫能誰何而方鎭
===
之勢遂不可復其患在士卒驕悍而難馴
乾符間王僊芝黃巢之徒流劫郡縣剽攻
國都天下騷動而唐遂以改步其患在盜
賊蠭起而不可禁遏宋之立國固已弱矣
其後捐靈武以畀夏割河東以畀遼及靖
康之後偏安江左不能復中原尺寸之地
其患在棄險資敵而不能自振此五患者
漢晉唐宋被之矣彼平居無事或疎於却
慮或墮於偷成迨乎縣寓多故干戈相尋

punctuated: 奚將焉恃乎？蓋自漢而下，凡爲天下大患者五：孝景時，吳、楚七國連兵內嚮，天子爲屈意誅謀臣謝過，空國都而拒戰，僅乃勝之，何岌岌也！其患在諸侯王强大而不軌。魏、晉以來，羌、胡、鮮卑降者，率居塞內諸郡。劉淵一倡，而幷、雍之胡響臻，神州遂陸沉矣。其患在華夷雜處而疎於防。唐自太和以後，士卒殺主帥、邀節鉞，若盧龍、陝虢、宣武諸軍，比比而是，朝廷莫能誰何，而方鎭之勢遂不可復。其患在士卒驕悍而難馴。乾符間，王僊芝、黃巢之徒，流劫郡縣，剽攻國都，天下騷動，而唐遂以改步。其患在盜賊蠭起而不可禁遏。宋之立國固已弱矣，其後捐靈武以畀夏，割河東以畀遼，及靖康之後，偏安江左，不能復中原尺寸之地。其患在棄險資敵而不能自振。此五患者，漢、晉、唐、宋被之矣。彼平居無事，或疎於却慮，或墮於偷成，迨乎縣寓多故，干戈相尋，
translation_en: …crisis [奚 for 急?], what then can be relied upon? Broadly speaking, from the Han dynasty onward, there have been five great perils to the realm. In the time of Emperor Xiaojing, the seven feudatory states led by Wu and Chu joined forces and marched inward. The Son of Heaven had to Humble himself to execute his advising minister in apology, and emptied the capital to mount a defense, barely managing to defeat them—how precarious that was! That peril lay in the feudatory princes being overly powerful and seditious. From the Wei and Jin onward, surrendered Qiang, Hu, and Xianbei peoples generally resided in the commanderies inside the frontier passes. Once Liu Yuan劉淵 raised the call, the Hu of Bingzhou and Yongzhou flocked to him in response, and the sacred heartland of China was utterly submerged. That peril lay in Chinese and barbarians living intermingled while defenses were lax. In the Tang, after the Taihe reign (827–835), soldiers murdered their commanders-in-chief and extorted the emblems of military governors; in armies such as Lulong, Shanguo, and Xuanwu, this happened everywhere. The court could do nothing about them, and control over the regional military commands could never be recovered. That peril lay in the troops being arrogant, fierce, and difficult to tame. During the Qianfu reign (874–879), men like Wang Xianzhi 王僊芝 and Huang Chao 黃巢 roamed and plundered the commanderies and counties and assaulted the imperial capital, throwing the empire into turmoil, whereby the Tang dynasty ultimately met its end. That peril lay in bandits swarming up like bees and being impossible to suppress. The Song dynasty was already weak from its very founding; afterward it abandoned Lingwu to the Xia and ceded Hedong to the Liao, and after the Jingkang catastrophe (1126–1127) it held onto a rump regime east of the Yangtze, unable to recover a single inch of the Central Plains. That peril lay in abandoning strategic strongholds to the benefit of the enemy and being unable to rouse itself. These five perils were suffered by the Han, Jin, Tang, and Song. In ordinary times of peace, they were either negligent in far-sighted planning or lapsed into complacent satisfaction with the status quo; by the time the realm was beset by troubles and warfare followed incessantly,…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
叱咤徒勤枝柱不遑此皆禍發于不虞而
釀成于所忽者也我
國家治臻上理運際休期天下稱至寧矣而
於此五者蓋亦有之寘鐇稱兵于寧夏宸
濠搆逆于南昌夫非七國之孽乎然而怒
臂當車崇朝翦滅磐石之宗猶故也三輔
之內號爲忠順軍者二萬騎夫非羌胡
雜處之轍乎然而屯牧分成以彈壓相參弭
耳伏喙猶故也雲中五堡之卒留都振武
===
之軍磔殺大臣必釀重禍鎮兵不驕悍乎
然而尺一朝馳譁伍夕定帖服猶故也劉
齊煽于近郊藍鄢猖于蜀漢蹂躪數省血
人于牙盜賊不蠭起乎然而偏師向往隨
熾輒撲按堵猶故也大寧徙而開平棄東
勝撤而河套失不以險資敵乎然而名王
請臣元戎奏捷幅幀猶故也夫在前代以
之危亂而
國家無損於治安兼被其患而終不能爲患

punctuated: 叱咤徒勤，枝柱不遑，此皆禍發于不虞，而釀成于所忽者也。我國家治臻上理，運際休期，天下稱至寧矣，而於此五者，蓋亦有之。寘鐇稱兵于寧夏，宸濠搆逆于南昌，夫非七國之孽乎？然而怒臂當車，崇朝翦滅，磐石之宗猶故也。三輔之內，號爲忠順軍者二萬騎，夫非羌、胡雜處之轍乎？然而屯牧分成，以彈壓相參，弭耳伏喙猶故也。雲中五堡之卒，留都振武之軍，磔殺大臣，必釀重禍，鎮兵不驕悍乎？然而尺一朝馳，譁伍夕定，帖服猶故也。劉、齊煽于近郊，藍、鄢猖于蜀、漢，蹂躪數省，血人于牙，盜賊不蠭起乎？然而偏師向往，隨熾輒撲，按堵猶故也。大寧徙而開平棄，東勝撤而河套失，不以險資敵乎？然而名王請臣，元戎奏捷，幅幀猶故也。夫在前代以之危亂，而國家無損於治安，兼被其患而終不能爲患，
translation_en:
… shouting in anger proved to be effort in vain, and there was no time left even to prop things up. All of these were disasters that erupted from the unexpected and brewed out of what was neglected.

Our dynasty’s governance has reached the highest order, its destiny meets with an auspicious era, and the realm is acclaimed as supremely tranquil; yet as for these five afflictions, it too has indeed experienced them. When Zhu Zhifan 朱寘鐇 raised troops in Ningxia 寧夏 and Zhu Chenhao 朱宸濠 plotted rebellion in Nanchang 南昌, were they not the evil sprouts of the Seven Kingdoms? Yet like a mantis angrily raising its forelegs to block a chariot, they were wiped out in a single morning, and the imperial clan—firm as a great rock—remained just as before. Within the Three Metropolitan Areas around the capital, those known as the Loyal and Obedient Armies (Zhongshun jun) number twenty thousand cavalry—is this not the same rut as the Qiang and Hu peoples living interspersed among the Chinese? Yet because farming colonies, pastures, and garrison posts are intermingled to hold them in check, they keep their ears flattened and their mouths bowed to the ground just as before. When the soldiers of the Five Forts in Yunzhong 雲中 and the troops of the Zhenwu Division in the Auxiliary Capital dismembered and murdered high ministers, bound to brew grave disaster, were the garrison soldiers not arrogant and fierce? Yet once an imperial edict of a foot and an inch sped forth in the morning, the mutinous ranks were pacified by evening, submissive and docile just as before. When Liu 六 [Liu Chong 劉寵] and Qi 齊 [Qi Yanming 齊彥明] fanned flames of revolt in the capital’s outskirts, and Lan 藍 [Lan Tingrui 藍廷瑞] and Yan 鄢 [Yan Ben恕 鄢本恕] ran rampant in Shu 蜀 and Hanzhong 漢, trampling several provinces and staining their fangs with human blood, did bandits and rebels not rise up in swarms? Yet wherever detachments of our army marched, no sooner had the blaze flared up than it was stamped out, and the populace remained undisturbed inside their walls just as before. When Daning 大寧 was relocated and Kaiping 開平 abandoned, and when Dongsheng 東勝 was withdrawn and the Ordos Loop (Hetao 河套) lost, was this not ceding strategic passes to aid the enemy? Yet famous chieftains have begged to submit as vassals, supreme commanders have reported victories, and the breadth of our territory remains just as before.

Now, why is it that what brought peril and disorder to former dynasties has caused no harm to the peace and order of our State, and though we have suffered all of these afflictions together, in the end they have been unable to become true calamities…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
此曷故焉懸蓋反覆求之矣農夫之治田
也反土而菑濬畎而溉荒也薙之莠也鋤
之故饑饉可無憂焉何也則圖之者豫也
善攝生者郛郭欲强腸胃欲實一受病不
遠千里而求醫師欲辟除而坐愈何也則
慮之者深也人君保乂天下之道胡以異
此往代罹患而不能支者非皆天事與人
力不勝也無乃國勢不重乎則偏而不舉
漸至積弱將束手待之矣無乃人心不安
===
乎則渙而不萃遇有急難將掉臂去之矣
此之為患又將誰咎耶
高皇帝總羣策奠八埏博稽逖覽創制立法樹
藩垣以衛根本辨封域以備羯夷肅軍伍
以震威稜據阨塞以壯形勢軫農桑以敦
本業祈噗溢以拊捐瘠其綰結約束者甚
詳而溫飫煦養者又甚溥蓋尊在
九重戴在四海國勢何重也徹乎肺腑通乎閭
閻人心何安也二百年來憑藉者厚而封

漸至積弱將束手待之矣無乃人心不安

===
此之爲患又將誰咎耶
高皇帝總羣策奠八埏博稽遐覽創制立法樹
藩垣以衛根本辨封域以備羯羠肅軍伍
以震威稜據阨塞以壯形勢軫農桑以敦
本業祈暵溢以拊捐瘠其綰結約束者甚
詳而溫飫煦養者又甚溥蓋尊在
九重戴在四海國勢何重也徹乎肺腑通乎閭
閻人心何安也二百年來憑藉者厚而封
punctuated: 此曷故焉？懸蓋反覆求之矣。農夫之治田也，反土而菑，濬畎而溉，荒也薙之，莠也鋤之，故饑饉可無憂焉，何也？則圖之者豫也。善攝生者，郛郭欲强，腸胃欲實，一受病，不遠千里而求醫，師欲辟除而坐愈，何也？則慮之者深也。人君保乂天下之道，胡以異此？往代罹患而不能支者，非皆天事與人力不勝也。無乃國勢不重乎？則偏而不舉，漸至積弱，將束手待之矣。無乃人心不安乎？則渙而不萃，遇有急難，將掉臂去之矣。此之為患，又將誰咎耶？高皇帝總羣策，奠八埏，博稽逖覽，創制立法：樹藩垣以衛根本，辨封域以備羯夷，肅軍伍以震威稜，據阨塞以壯形勢，軫農桑以敦本業，祈噗溢以拊捐瘠。其綰結約束者甚詳，而溫飫煦養者又甚溥。蓋尊在九重，戴在四海，國勢何重也！徹乎肺腑，通乎閭閻，人心何安也！二百年來，憑藉者厚而封
translation_en:
… Why is this so? I [?; 懸, likely misprint for 愚] have repeatedly sought the reason for it. When a farmer tends his fields, he turns the soil to break new ground and dredges the furrows to irrigate; where it is overgrown with weeds he clears it, and where there are tares he hoes them out. Thus he need have no worry of famine. Why is this? Because he plans for it beforehand. One who is skilled at nurturing life wishes his outer frame to be strong and his bowels and stomach to be solid; the moment he contracts an illness, he does not consider a thousand li too far to seek a physician, wishing to dispel the malady and recover with ease. Why is this? Because his forethought is deep. How does the ruler's way of preserving and governing the realm differ from this? When past dynasties suffered calamities and could not sustain themselves, it was not always because of Heaven's affairs or because human strength was unequal to the task. Was it not rather that the prestige and momentum of the state lacked weight? Then it became lopsided and could not be lifted, gradually sinking into accumulated weakness until they could only bind their hands and await their fate. Or was it not that the minds of the people were unsettled? Then they scattered and could not be gathered together, so that when an emergency arose, they simply swung their arms and walked away. When such things become a calamity, whom else is there to blame?

The Exalted Emperor (Gao Huangdi, i.e., Emperor Taizu) gathered together all counsels and settled the eight extremities of the world; examining broadly and surveying afar, he founded institutions and established laws. He erected princely screen-walls to guard the fundamental core, demarcated the borderlands to prepare against the northern and western barbarians, enforced strictness in the military ranks to project awe-inspiring majesty, occupied strategic passes to strengthen the topographical advantage, showed solicitude for agriculture and sericulture to encourage the fundamental occupations, and prayed [?] [祈噗溢, likely a garbled transcription of 蠲租賦 "remitted taxes and levies" or similar] to comfort the destitute and emaciated. That by which he bound and regulated the realm was most detailed, and that by which he warmly nourished and nurtured it was most廣泛 (universal). Indeed, with supreme authority residing in the Ninefold Palace and allegiance held throughout the Four Seas, how weighty was the prestige of the state! Reaching deep into people's hearts and extending throughout the village lanes, how settled were the minds of the people! For two hundred years, what has been relied upon is thick and what has been built up and…

title: 萬曆八年會試錄
text:
殖者深雖有逆藩巨寇強胡悍卒冒法而
犯科懷奸而伺釁一剗刈之天下晏如矣
蓋前代所以危亂咎在本實先撥無以待
天下之患而
國家所以治安要在豐基強榦患至而有以
應之此其大較也抑愚聞之事之適變也
若地形然機漸以往俄而東西易面人不
自知也故弭患於未形而制變於先事則
在國勢常重人心常安而已凡上之所以
===
使下而臂指相運者紀綱正也紀綱若銜
轡欲謹操之無令縱弛然命令不審則或
泥而不行賞罰不明則或玩而不肅法伸
於微弱而詘於貴強則亡徒有以窺權白
黑變於下而取舍不制於上則奸人得以
投隙此縱弛之漸也惟惕然振飭有頓網
挈裘之體無旁落倒持之嫌有風行雷動
之威無拘文牽俗之陋則天下奉法承式
孰不凛然畏而守之乎紀綱正而國勢有

punctuated: 殖者深，雖有逆藩、巨寇、強胡、悍卒冒法而犯科，懷奸而伺釁，一剗刈之，天下晏如矣。蓋前代所以危亂，咎在本實先撥，無以待天下之患；而國家所以治安，要在豐基強榦，患至而有以應之，此其大較也。抑愚聞之，事之適變也，若地形然，機漸以往，俄而東西易面，人不自知也。故弭患於未形，而制變於先事，則在國勢常重、人心常安而已。凡上之所以使下而臂指相運者，紀綱正也。紀綱若銜轡，欲謹操之，無令縱弛。然命令不審，則或泥而不行；賞罰不明，則或玩而不肅；法伸於微弱而詘於貴強，則亡徒有以窺權；白黑變於下而取舍不制於上，則奸人得以投隙，此縱弛之漸也。惟惕然振飭，有頓網挈裘之體，無旁落倒持之嫌；有風行雷動之威，無拘文牽俗之陋，則天下奉法承式，孰不凛然畏而守之乎？紀綱正而國勢有

… cultivated is deep. Even when there were rebellious princedoms, great bandits, powerful northern nomads, or unruly soldiers who braved the law and violated the statutes, harboring treachery and watching for an opening, once they were mowed down, the realm remained tranquil. Indeed, the reason former dynasties fell into peril and disorder was the fault of their root and substance being first uprooted, leaving them with nothing to meet the calamities of the world; whereas the essential reason our dynasty enjoys peace and order lies in enriching the foundation and strengthening the trunk, having the means to respond when calamities arrive. This is the broad outline of the matter.

Yet I, in my simplicity, have heard that when affairs move toward change, it is like the terrain of the land: the mechanism advances gradually, and suddenly east and west have switched faces without people realizing it themselves. Therefore, to quell calamities before they take form and to control change prior to events lies simply in keeping the national momentum ever weighty and popular sentiment ever secure.

Whenever the ruler is able to command his subordinates so that they operate together like arm and finger, it is because the laws and discipline are upright. Laws and discipline are like bit and reins: one wishes to hold them carefully and never let them go slack. Yet if orders and commands are not carefully deliberated, they may become bogged down and not be carried out; if rewards and punishments are not clear, they may be trifled with and lack rigor; if the law is enforced upon the humble and weak but bends before the noble and powerful, then lawless scoundrels will have a way to spy upon authority; if black and white are inverted below while acceptance and rejection are not controlled from above, then treacherous persons will manage to exploit the cracks. These are the gradual beginnings of slackening. Only if one vigilantly rouses and rectifies things—maintaining the form of jerking the head-rope of a net or lifting a fur coat by the collar, without the suspicion of power slipping away or holding the sword by the blade; possessing the majesty of wind sweeping and thunder rolling, without the pettiness of being bound by empty words or dragged along by vulgar custom—then throughout the realm, in observing the laws and receiving the standards, who will not stand in awe and abide by them? When laws and discipline are upright, could the national momentum…
